entry.title: The Ban Hammer Has Spoken
entry.content:
Earlier this month, Instagram permanently banned me.

What Happened?

On the evening of the 1st of November, I was in my Instagram DMs when I got a message on WhatsApp saying my Instagram account was temporarily disabled. When I switched back to Instagram, it said the same thing, and asked me to verify my identity. I chose the recommended selfie verification option where had to show my face from different angles, and then waited for the account to be reinstated.
About half an hour later, I got an email saying it was permanently disabled.

Crisis Management

The Instagram app said my account was permanently disabled, and that I couldn't appeal this decision. So I would need some way to reach out to my Instagram-only contacts and let them know what happened.
Luckily, there was a data download option, where I could download all the data instagram had on me. That way, I could reach out to anyone I wanted from a different account.
I clicked on that data download option and they said it would be in my email in 30 days. While writing this post, on the 27th of November, I requested another data download and got the link via email after half an hour. The download process beyond the link was undocumented and unintuitive. And the information in the download tells me that this is the data from the 27th, not from the 1st.

Under "How We Made This Decision", it simply said "or technology found your account doesn't follow our rules and as a result it took action".
Wonderful. A permanent decision made by a bot with no human oversight.

But What Violation?

I had a few hypotheses.

Harassment

I was chatting with someone I had met on Hinge at the moment I got that fateful WhatsApp message. Did I say something unacceptable?
Well this obviously couldn't be the reason I was banned because she would've needed superhuman speeds to report me, in the unlikely event that I actually did something worth reporting.

Politics

Okay then, I got permabanned because of the political stuff I was sharing.
Really? On a private account? When all the accounts I reshared stuff from are still running?

Patched APK

I used a patched version of the instagram app that stripped out all ads and recommended content. I thought that was only client-side patching and the server shouldn't know, but maybe I was wrong?
But then the only reason they'd know I wasn't looking at ads and suggested content was… just the number of times my account requested ads and suggested content. Which shouldn't have been too low because I had been spending more time than I liked doomscrolling in the browser.

Arbitrary And Capricious

At this point, it hit me. I would never know why I was banned. I wouldn't, because Instagram had not given me a support contact or an avenue to appeal. Even if they had, customer support for nearly every company has been useless lately. If they exist, they exist because they have a legal requirement to exist, and they are only given the tools to blame the user for every problem.

I also decided not to make a new Instagram account because, well, why would I? I had no interest in begging for access to a platform where I was kicked out with zero provided justification, zero chance of appeal, and heck zero human oversight, only to spend every future moment on the platform worried about what I did wrong the last time and how I can be a good boy this time around.

Why Was An Anti-Big-Tech Blogger On Instagram In The First Place?

I did consider deleting my account multiple times. But ultimately I decided to use an APK stripped of everything I hate about Instagram because it was a useful, low-effort tool to stay updated with what was going on in my friends' lives.
How will I replace that? I don't know yet.

entry.title: Formula One Ran So AI Regulators Could Stumble Along
entry.content:
Here are some similarities between Formula One racing and frontier AI research:

  • They are both principally engineering competitions at the frontier of technology. They both involve a small number of extremely well-resourced, sophisticated firms, deploying highly motivated teams trying to make largely the same product (single-seater racing cars, large language models).
  • They both involve enormous capital expenditure to maintain tiny performance advantages that can shift from week to week. They can both have very short technological cycles, in which a dominant competitive advantage can disappear in a matter of months.
  • They both involve perpetually trying to poach one another’s engineers, sometimes paying extraordinary sums for particular individuals.
  • They both involve complicated relationships with a small number of suppliers of critical technological components.
  • They both perform elaborate public rituals for unveiling their latest products, accompanied by carefully selected statistics that sometimes unravel in actual field performance.
  • They both have extremely engaged communities of technically literate spectators who speculate about engineering decisions on the basis of incomplete public information.
  • They both have a history of extraordinarily wealthy people deciding that they would like to have a team of their own.
  • They both involve balancing performance on well-understood metrics (lap times, benchmarks) with poorly understood safety risks that might result from that performance (killing several people, armageddon).
  • They both have access to a finite quantity of extremely expensive engineering resources (wind tunnel time, compute), and a substantial part of the engineering challenge consists in determining how best to allocate those resources between competing avenues of technological development.
  • They both have decadent, silly European regulators. They both have teams that claim that they need further regulation in order to mitigate safety risks, sometimes earnestly, and sometimes tactically to preserve a competitive advantage.

The last two similarities are converging. Proposals for AI regulation are beginning to sound eerily similar to the FIA, the F1 regulator. Some ideas on how to pace the frontier involve a primitive regulatory notion that you shouldn’t try to regulate a hazard directly, but should reach for the most regulatable ‘control surface’ near it.

In modern Formula One, which is a lot about aerodynamics, one of the inputs is wind tunnel time. New wings, floors and sidepods are developed and then tested in wind tunnels. Teams used to run tunnels unrestricted, ‘24 hours a day, seven days a week’, to find tenths of a second. The FIA today has ‘aerodynamic testing restrictions’ which cap wind tunnel runs. The leading team gets the smallest allowance, and the last-placed team gets the largest. There’s also a budget cap.

With AI research, regulating compute is the obvious choice. Scaling laws tie a model’s capabilities closely to the compute spent on pretraining it. That compute is scarce: the chips come from a supply chain that runs through a tiny number of firms. FLOP counts are far easier to verify and coordinate around than assessments of model behaviour. And so here’s a recent proposal from the AI Futures Project:

The first component is Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD): AI companies regularly disclose their compute usage, and an independent auditor verifies the disclosures. The second component is to reallocate compute away from capabilities R&D and toward other use cases, such as serving customers and safety research (non-capabilities R&D).

More aggressive proposals suggest moving frontier AI research to an FIA-style regulatory cycle. A post on the EA Forum last year, titled Rolling Thresholds for AGI Scaling Regulation, would put every lab on one shared calendar:

The plan revolves around a unified schedule for model scaling across different companies.

All companies intending to train cutting-edge models must submit pre-registered plans to the regulator, detailing expected model behavior and clearly defined criteria for halting training runs in case of unexpected issues.

On January 1st, the regulator lifts the training run maximum size limit, allowing the training of these pre-registered models up to a new certain size (e.g. level of flops, number of parameters) to commence.

AI 2040: Plan A scales the same idea up into a deal between the US and China, built on each side declaring its compute and sharing all AI research:

Their rationales for regulation could not be more different. Formula One regulation wants a level-ish playing field between competitors. AI regulation wants to prevent superintelligent god machines from destroying the world. But the proposed mechanisms of regulation end up looking very similar.

entry.title: Weekly Notes 48/2026
entry.content:
For most of the week, I was in Ahmedabad/Gujarat spending time with the extended Pucar community here. I got time to work with them, run some sessions, and learn about their working style. Just that the travel was a bit hectic; otherwise, it was fun.

  • My RIPE Atlas probe has been online for 4 years now. Its uptime is 84.34%. Not great, but not bad.
  • I did a bit of walking/running this week, but not enough. I plan to go back to P.T. sessions from next week.
  • I don’t know if anyone knows what’s happening in the Indian stock market. I am a passive, mostly an index fund investor. The movements in the markets are so frequent and so random that even I get to know about them :) Also, there is no way to invest in US or Asian funds easily anymore due to SEBI limitations. I have no idea why they make it so difficult for ordinary Indians. Of course, there are other, less easy ways. I am trying Parag Parikh IFSC S&P 500 Fund of Fund, which goes through GIFT City. But it’s very cumbersome “just” to invest. I am not sure how complex it will be during tax returns. Ideally, I would like 25% of my whole portfolio outside India, with 20% of that in the USA. But it’s not easy to maintain that ratio. This is not advice. This is just airing my problem.
  • I am reading Telling the Truth to Your Adopted or Foster Child: Making Sense of the Past. I am yet to complete it. Many parts of it are also heavily focused on the Western form of adoption and can’t be directly applied to Indian parents. That said, it has some valuable pointers for us too. I will write a detailed review later.
  • Also started reading ಭಾರತೀಪುರ (Bharathipura English translation on Archive). I’m reading just a chapter per day before going to sleep. And bought ಭಗವಂತನ ಸಾವು (Bhagavantana Saavu is a translation of K R Meera’s Bhagavante Maranam translated to Kannada). Fellow Bangalore blogger Jatin has published an ebook about Chandrayaan called Crafty Moon-craft. I haven’t read it yet, but it’s on my list.
  • We watched Jailer 2 on Sunday. That took 3 hours away from my sleep. But we had not seen any movies together in a long time. Given that this was successful. It’s an average movie.
  • Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights, so basically they can make themselves better or worse. WetBrain is an Open source AI browser agent for chatting with pages, automating tasks, and running multi-step workflows with your choice of LLM. You can use your local local llama.cpp models with it.

You can read this blog using RSS Feed. But if you are the person who loves getting emails, then you can join my readers by signing up.

entry.title: Curiosity starts it, habit keeps it
entry.content:
Today was mostly work again, but the good kind. Something new and exciting started, and I kept digging without needing any push. Curiosity was both the cue and the reward, so the research ran on its own.

But excitement has a short shelf life. The new thing stops being new, and then the digging stops too, unless it has become a habit by then. A fixed hour of reading and noting, every day, long after the thrill has gone.

Richard Hamming puts it well in You and Your Research:

Given two people with exactly the same ability, the one person who manages day in and day out to get in one more hour of thinking will be tremendously more productive over a lifetime.

  • Richard Hamming

entry.title: Udupi Mangalore Trip Day 1
entry.content:
I recently (2nd-4th October 2026) went on a three day trip to Sakleshpur, Udupi and Mangalore. This post is a first installment in a three part blog series detailing my adventures.

How did it come to be?

Soumyadeep is the brain behind this trip. He and I have been friends since our JEE coaching days (junior college/11th-12th standard). We met each other randomly in a sharing rickshaw one day. We realized we were in the same class and heading in the same direction. From that point onwards, we travelled back to the railway station together after classes.

My home was near the railway station, but he travelled from a different city altogether! This is the reality of entrance exams in this country, kids are made to travel vast distances every single day in hopes of making it big someday. He recognized this was a hassle but never complained about it.

We used to talk about the most random ass shit on the ride back. This continued for two years. Small enough time to be a passing by phase in life. Thankfully, our friendship wasn't. Few people stay. Soumyadeep has been one of them. We literally have nothing in common, our degrees, professions, interests, residence, none. Though, none of that has stopped us from staying in touch!

And hence, when he told me he was coming to Bengaluru for a conference, I already knew how he was spending the rest of his stay. He then pitched the trip and that's how it came to be. We decided the long weekend of 2nd to 4th October would be the perfect time. Another local friend of his named Rakesh decided to join us. And so the planning began! Rakesh wanted to do the Ettina Bhuja hike and Soumyadeep wanted to enjoy Udupi and Mangalore. With places decided, Soumyadeep took on the responsibility of travel. He booked the outward and return trains. Rakesh handled the trek tickets. And I was in charge of hotel bookings...which I conveniently forgot about. 🙈

Brave on dose

Our train to Sakleshpur was supposed to arrive at Yewanthpur by 05:45. It was early in the morning and we didn't want to risk it, so we pre-booked an Uber the night before. We reached early enough and had some time to spare. Both of us were yawning uncontrollably and hence decided to prepare our sleep-deprived bodies for the upcoming long day with a coffee!

We headed to a darshini nearby and ordered masala doses with some hot filter coffee. By the time our first two doses arrived, Rakesh was there too! This was my first time meeting him in person. Walking into the conversation, I had a bad mental image. I have known quite a few people named Rakesh, and all of them have been A-rated evil people. Thankfully, this Rakesh broke all the bad assumptions. In hindsight, I should have known this, considering he is Soumyadeep's good friend.

By the time we completed some small talk over food, we realized there were 20 minutes left for the train's departure. But then I noticed Soumyadeep hadn't had his dose. We were never delivered the third dose!! As it was a self-service system, we looked over the counter, and realized it had gotten so crowded that they had lost the track of our third dose. Soumyadeep grew reluctant to get it cause of the train, but I also knew he was super hungry from our earlier conversations in the cab.

I am usually not an outgoing person, but certain circumstances open the pathway to let my demons out. "WE HAVE PAID FOR IT, WE WILL GET IT". With that slogan, I rushed to the counter. Sadly, the crowd wasn't forgiving. I had to argue with the owner to get the food we had paid for half an hour prior! Thankfully, it arrived in time and we were able to catch the train.

A heated start to the trip, definitely not a bad omen.

Ettina Bhuja

We found this interesting poster on the train:

What about it is interesting you ask? Universities advertising AI in their courseware? Assured 100% placement guarantee? Nah, look at the HCL logo in the right hand side corner.

We caught up on sleep on the train and reached Sakleshpur by 11:00. Ettina Bhuja is around 30-40 km away from the main city and hence we needed a rickshaw to reach there. We tried haggling with rickshaw drivers outside the railway station, but they were too rude for us to continue. This is a pretty common occurrence with non-Kannada speakers, but in this case we had pushed Rakesh ahead to talk. And he's a local guy! After the unsuccessful attempt at getting a ride, we decided to walk to the bus station and try finding a ride from there.

Sakleshpur's bus station is around 1.2 km away from the railway station. Displacement between both is super small, but the distance is long because of a lake. It was a nice walk around the lake and luckily we found a rickshaw driver willing to take us at reasonable prices. I covered the rest of the hike experience in this blog here.

After an exhausting hike, I was already feeling super groggy. Hence we decided to stop for a coffee on our way back. It was a random cafe in the middle of nowhere. I wasn't expecting much, but even that wasn't enough. Their coffee was amongst the worst coffee I have ever had! Absolute lowest in the charts. Something I find puzzling: there's filter coffee everywhere in and around Bengaluru. What is up with Sakleshpur? There was no good coffee to be found! I am pretty sure a lot of coffee grows in that area cause I could see plantations en route to the hike. Sadly, locals don't seem interested in sipping some of their harvest.

It didn't help that our last meal was 05:00 in the morning. At this point, we were in dire need of some good food. We asked for the best local darshini around, of which there was just one open on that day. For what seemed like a never ending order, we got a nice smile from the waiter for giving them some business :). It was around 16:00, well pass lunchtime. The kitchen didn't have a lot of ingredients prepared and ready to be used. As they were taking their own sweet time to prepare our order, I was determined to get the taste of that coffee out my mouth immediately. Fortunately, just before entering the darshini, I had noticed a bakery nearby. And with sheer luck, a Cream Bun food critic found its perfect target. Learning from my previous mistakes I kept my expectations absolutely low. Good thing I did. I would rate it 2.5/5. 0.5 brownie points for it finding me at the point I needed it the most!

Our next order of business was figuring out where to go. As we hadn't planned anything, we could go to Udupi or Mangalore either. Worst part, we kept swinging between both options. None of us was able to decid what to do 😭. Best potential tie breaker was going to be us finding an accommodation in Shri Krishna Matha in Udupi. Sadly, even that fell through. In the end, we played choose-a-finger game and boarded a bus to Mangalore! Thought, we were yet to figure out an accommodation.

Let us in

We had just boarded the bus and had some spare energy from the recent gluttonous attack on food. This energy was beamed at finding hotels in Mangalore. We opened maps, searched for all the hotels available and started calling them one after the other. "No room saar" beep beep. After hearing that around 20-30 times, it started to dawn upon us: we might be in a hairy situation regarding accommodation. It was not wise to underestimate the long weekend. We finally decided to give up on calling and planned on asking rickshaw drivers to take us to different hotels they have tie up with. Maybe all we need is an inside agent, who takes some commission, but gets the job done. After so many conversations, my social battery was dead. Just in time, insulin spike gently carried me into a nice nap.

We reached Mangalore around 21:00. Time to pour the regained energy into accommodation hunt! We started knocking on doors of all the hotels near the bus stand. There was some hope in doing this cause a bunch of them weren't listed on Google Maps. To our dismay, none had any rooms left. Soumyadeep was checking hotel listings on MakeMyTrip and one of the owners was responding very positively. In desperation, we decided to go to the rough location provided by the in-app map. A bunch of lost boys, walking around the locality, trying to hang onto this sliver of hope. It appeared we were getting close to the guest house and owner was responding nicely, almost offering us a booking. No jinx, please? please? When we finally got owner's contact and were about to tell him that we are ready to check in, he cancelled the booking 😭.

Okay, now our only hopes are rickshaw drivers. Ma Messiah. We found a guy and asked him to show us hotels nearby. He drove us around ~2km away, towards the center of the city. We stopped at a decent looking hotel in the middle of a one way road. This time we had more than a sliver, this was an industrial thread. It was woven by driver's boasts about his personal relations here. He had called and asked about empty rooms before accepting the ride. Guess what? It was FULL too! Fuck this shit. At this point, Rakesh was half panicking. We started walking alongside the road, and I spotted a rusty board advertising a hotel. This ain't no mirage. The rundown building we were looking at had few of its floors converted into a hotel. To reach reception, we had to enter a super shady looking basement. I started preparing to make a deal with the devil.

Guess what? This was FULL too! Or so the receptionist said. This is where it gets interesting and something I have learnt about from this experience. Mid-tier hotels will always say there are no empty rooms during rush hours. But if you insist enough and walk with one of the employees to see a room at higher rates/higher grade, he might sneakily offer you a deal. In our case, receptionist said he only had an expensive "suite" available. We walked with the doorman to see the room. Once we were inside, he offered us an AC room on the same floor! Ma Messiah!

He asked us to quote a price and I didn't want to lose this opportunity. Naturally, I quoted a slightly higher rate. In hindsight, I could have haggled and received the room for a much lower price. Lessons learnt.

And hence, we finally found a temporary place to call home sweet home for the next two days.

Shake dat

We all freshened up and were ready to put the tummy growls at rest. Rakesh was somehow hungry enough that he wanted to have a complete biryani! I cannot finish a full serving of biryani even on the best of my days. Soumyadeep and I weren't as hungry. We decided to have a small shake and a few fries at a nearby cafe called Shake Factory. We ordered Nutty chocolate and Cream & Cookies shake alongside some loaded french fries.

Shakes were fantabulous. And the fries, oh boy they were loaded. Not just with toppings, but in quantity too 😭. Soumyadeep and I together barely finished the combo. We were so full, we had to take a 3-4 km walk around the city to feel better. At least this place isn't an active participant of shrinkflation yet :).

Loads of movement plus awesome food. Perfect recipe for a good night's sleep.

entry.title: When the hands know, the mind is free
entry.content:
My hands open reddit without asking me first. That is muscle memory, and it never asked whether Power of Habit was worth learning. The same hands can learn to open the agenda, capture a note, or start the day's work before the mind has finished making excuses.

Muscle memory does not replace focus, it frees it. A driver who no longer thinks about the gears can watch the road. When the routine runs on its own, focus chimes in for the part that actually needs thinking, and the work starts taking care of itself. As Bruce Lee is often quoted:

I fear not the man who has practiced 10,000 kicks once, but the man who has practiced one kick 10,000 times.

  • Bruce Lee

So the real question is not how to stay focused, but what I am training my hands to do while I am not looking. Get into the flow, not void.

of diamond studs
and pink rose buds

With a few faces of Frida!

entry.title: The Firms Just Want to Grow
entry.content:
One of the stupidest things about India is the firm size cliff.

The world, generally, does not produce cliffs like this. Cliffs like this—usually—need regulation to produce them. Take a look at the bar chart, and try to guess where most labour laws in India (in 2021-22) kicked in. If your guess was “10 workers”, then you’re right. Since then, a bunch of states have raised their thresholds. But think about how insane that is. This—successfully inhibiting firm size so that no one employs enough people to attract your regulation—is, to anyone, comprehensive evidence of the failure of a regulation.

Last year, the Labour Codes were brought into force. They consolidated 29 laws into four Codes. They relaxed some terrible things about Indian labour regulation, and introduced somewhat higher thresholds. But since they’re mainly a compilation of laws rather than a wholesale reimagining of Indian labour law, it is still far from a sane regime.

Actually, it’s worth reminding ourselves what the labour laws say. As Rajagopalan & Shah (2024) put it, ‘[i]nstead of setting basic standards for safety and hygiene, the regulations micromanage how firms keep their employees safe and punish firms—often through inspectors who demand bribes and foist criminal penalties—if that exact method is not followed.’ Examples:

  • “The Factories Act, 1948, mandates the provision of spittoons in convenient locations within factory premises, with state governments empowered to prescribe their type, number, and placement.”
  • “The act also requires construction establishments to provide “soft” and “absorbent” toilet paper and specifies that latrine and urinal floors and walls must be finished with glazed tiles or similar materials up to a height of 90 centimeters (Section 19).”
  • “The Minimum Wages Act, 1948, specifies colors for official register paper and ink (Section 18) while the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, dictates wage-slip font sizes (Section 6).”
  • “The excesses of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, are well documented; in addition to its rules on hiring, firing, and firm closure, it requires firms to get the government’s permission before they reassign workers to different tasks.”

Perhaps these rules sound like good ideas to some people. In a different, more communist life, I might have started a sentence that went: ‘reasonable people can disagree about whether firms should need government permission before they can reallocate their workers to different tasks.’ But this is not that life, and it was a little funny when the CPI(M)’s document ‘Labour Codes – Working People on the Warpath’ (Dec 11, 2025) talked about the raising of thresholds for the application of labour law before saying:

All these measures will push out thousands of more workers beyond the protection of laws.

‘Thousands’! No, really, ‘thousands’! In a country with a working age population of 1 billion and one of the lowest workforce productivity levels in the world. In Rajasthan, the thresholds for applying labour law got just a bit higher (from 10 workers to 20 workers). This led to ‘increases in both total output across the state and output per factory.’

There are lots of things preventing firms from scaling up in India. We need to fix all of them. Ilya said ‘the models just want to learn.’ The firms just want to grow. Large firms are good. When the firm gets larger, it achieves economies of scale. When the firm gets larger, it gets better access to credit. It invests in better processes and better equipment. It enters a virtuous cycle: more profit, more expansion, more hiring, more growth. Fixing the labour laws won’t get us there by default. But it would be nice if we could stop shooting ourselves in the foot every morning before we set out on the journey to development.

entry.title: Veg protein is all bloat
entry.content:
Rajma, dal, horsegram, tofu, chana, soya chunks. I have tried them all, and every one of them leaves me bloated for the whole day. Walking does not help, water does not help, and I spend the evening carrying a balloon I never ordered. If it does not affect you, you are lucky, so go build yourself better then, I'm not happy for you cause I'm bloat.

Eggs and chicken just work, no drama. Milk is the only veg protein I would still consider, but it brings its own fat along. The rest of my plate is sorted: carbs, fruits for fibre, vitamins and minerals. Protein is the only fight left, and with veg sources I end up bloated, not goated nor shredded.

entry.title: Power of Habit
entry.content:
Every good thing should be a habit, and every bad thing turns out to be a habit as well.

Habit is such a great quirk. I lately realised that whatever productivity hunt or anti-procrastination drive we go on, habit is the only de-facto solution there.

How I noticed it

I started realising this after reading the slides by yantar92 (Ihor Radchenko) for his EmacsConf 2026 talk, Personal task management under stress (with Org mode). He is the Org mode maintainer, and he does it in his spare time alongside a day job. I have been following him and attending the monthly Org meetup, and I am always astonished by how he even manages his life: so many emails on the Org mailing list that only he can take care of most of the time, work life, personal life, pending tasks and patches to review.

In the talk he outlines how tasks cannot be spread across different places like apps, the browser, email, your head, a notebook and maybe a phone call. They need one home. His first rule is simply "If you manage tasks in Org, do it in Org", and the second one is the one that stuck with me:

Task management won't work unless it becomes habit. Ever!

This is where Org mode and habit come into the picture.

The habit I already had

I noticed that I often open reddit (r/emacs, r/OnePiece and so on), lobste.rs, mastodon and many more tabs to catch up every day and see what is happening. This has become so habituated that every day, without any effort, my hands naturally takes me there. It is a three times a day thing: morning, lunch and late night. That can be put down to media craving, but that is another topic.

The key thing to notice is that it has no obstacle. It is never missed, there is no holding back, and even at the busiest time there is at least a glance over it. That is my habit, and it connected all my GTD thoughts, productivity, self-help and everything else. From that moment I made sure, and even configured my system, to make it a thorough habit to capture notes, schedule tasks every day and just get on with them.

What a habit is made of

Both popular books on this say roughly the same thing in simple words:

  • In The Power of Habit, Charles Duhigg describes a loop: a cue triggers a routine, and a reward tells the brain the loop is worth remembering. To change a habit, keep the cue and the reward and swap the routine.
  • In Tiny Habits, BJ Fogg says to make the new behaviour so small it needs no motivation, attach it to something you already do (an anchor: "After I …, I will …"), and celebrate it right away so it feels good.

Yantar's slides put the same idea in his own words: "Build new habits using existing habits". My tab ritual is a ready-made anchor. The cue (morning, lunch, night) and the reward (catching up) are already there, so the task habit only has to ride along with it.

Habits in Emacs and Org mode

This is what that looks like in plain Org, nothing fancy. It is the same idea as my Art of Getting things Done post: start with defaults and let the system evolve.

Capture everything into one inbox

The cheapest habit is capture. One key, one file, no thinking about where it goes. org-capture does this from anywhere in Emacs, and you sort it later. 

(setq org-capture-templates
      '(("i" "Inbox" entry (file "~/inbox.org")
         "* TODO %?\n%U")))
(keymap-global-set "C-c c" #'org-capture)
(keymap-global-set "M-k c" #'org-capture)
(keymap-global-set "s-k c" #'org-capture)
;; *-k since sounds like `K'apture

(keymap-global-set "M-j" #'org-agenda)
(keymap-global-set "s-j" #'org-agenda)
;; *-j since sounds like A`J'enda

The same inbox works on the phone with Emacs on Android or an Org app (bloom), and from the browser or elfeed or email notes.

Open the agenda before the tabs

This is the anchor. Before reddit, open org-agenda (M-j). It takes a few seconds and it tells you what today actually needs. Yantar splits his day view into "Must do today", "May do today" and "Can do on a good day", which keeps a bad day from turning into a guilty one.

Open it anywhere, everywhere and anytime, make it a rhythm and make it a habit

Track the habit itself with org-habit

Org has a built-in habit tracker. A habit is a TODO with a STYLE of habit and a repeater, and the agenda draws a small consistency graph next to it, so a broken streak is visible at a glance. 

(with-eval-after-load 'org
  (require 'org-habit))

* TODO Process inbox.org
  SCHEDULED: <2026-11-26 Thu .+1d>
  :PROPERTIES:
  :STYLE:    habit
  :END:
* TODO Catch up: r/emacs, lobste.rs
  SCHEDULED: <2026-11-26 Thu .+1d>
  :PROPERTIES:
  :STYLE:    habit
  :Effort:   0:20
  :END:

The second entry is my favourite idea from the talk: instead of fighting the distraction, give it its own habit with a time limit ("check social media (daily, once per day, 20 min max!)"). Clock in with C-c C-x C-i, and the Effort estimate tells you when to stop. A .+1d repeater means "one day after I last did it", and something like .+2d/4d allows a little slack for habits that are not strictly daily.

Review weekly, and plan to fall off

Daily habits keep things moving, and a weekly review keeps the list honest. Group the someday tasks under projects or topics so the review stays short, and trim what no longer matters.

Habits also break: a trip, an illness, a busy month. Yantar's fourth rule covers exactly this: "First, go back to the habit of using your task management". Do not rebuild the system, just open the agenda again tomorrow.

Closing

None of this needs a new app or a perfect setup. One plain text file (see Org mode is the best OBTF), one capture key, one agenda glance tied to a habit I already had. The tools only help once the habit is there.

The craft which

carrying five nations

with an ailing raft
 in a show of mastercraft

entry.title: CDs are great. Buying them in India isn’t
entry.content:
I recently went to Jakarta to catch a concert, and came back with about twenty CDs in my suitcase. New ones cost me between ₹1,000 and ₹2,000, used ones as little as ₹500, and I found them everywhere I looked. Back in India, the cheap CDs are mostly older catalogue and compilations, anything recent costs import prices, and you can only find them in a handful of online stores. I've gotten really into CDs lately, and I need to whine about how hard they are to buy in this country.

When I got my turntable, I wrote about why owning your music on physical media is worth it. The funny thing is that almost everything I said there applies to CDs even more. CD-quality audio has higher fidelity and dynamic range than vinyl ever will (I said it then and I stand by it), a CD doesn't wear out from being played, and a new CD costs a fraction of what a new LP costs in most places.

The compact disc is the pragmatic listener's physical format. Good luck buying one here.

India's CD era was a blip

CDs did sell here for a while, just mostly not the legal kind. The real CD scene in India was the bootleg one: burned discs and "Top 100 Hits" MP3 compilations from the guy at the market, for a fraction of what a real album cost. I don't think my father bought a single legit CD after I was five. Planet M had racks of the real thing, which most people walked past because they were "expensive".

So the legitimate CD never became the way India listened to music like how the cassette was. It was a brief stop between cassettes and MP3s, and then streaming. Shridhar Subramaniam, then head of Sony Music India, has said that India was never a CD market.

According to IFPI data, Indian CD sales halved in just three years, from 41.6 million units in 2012 to 21.4 million in 2015. For a country of over a billion people, even the peak was modest, and it collapsed fast.

Planet M and the other music retail chains died. Labels stopped pressing anything beyond a short new-release window. And when the physical media revival finally arrived, it went straight to vinyl and skipped the CD entirely. So now LPs cost more than ₹4k, and the format that could have been the cheap way to own music just isn't here.

Jakarta spoiled me

What stuck with me about Jakarta wasn't any single purchase, it was how normal it all was. You walk into a store and there's a wall of CDs, new and used, at prices that are reasonable, even when converted to INR. Indonesia kept its CD culture, while India lost whatever it had.

Some of what I bought there was available in India at reasonable prices, like Plastic Beach, so: egg on my face. But I wouldn't have thought to buy them at all if I hadn't seen them on a shelf, and would’ve had to buy Van Halen’s 1978 debut new instead of used.

What buying a CD in India looks like

Your options, as far as I've found:

  • Music Circle: a Mumbai record shop with an online store. It's mostly known for secondhand vinyl, but it also sells new and pre-owned CDs across rock, jazz, Bollywood, Indian classical, ghazals and more. This is the one store with good prices (Indian collectors on Reddit agree), with plenty of unused CDs going for around ₹400. They're old stock rather than new pressings, probably made in 2015 at the latest, so the catalogue leans older (Elvis, Santana, the Black Eyed Peas, lots of compilations). Still, it's the closest thing to browsing a CD rack in India right now.
  • The Revolver Club: a record and hi-fi store with outlets in many cities, that sells online. It's vinyl first, but it stocks some CDs as well, mostly priced under ₹2,000–3,000 apart from a few outliers. From the look of it, the CD catalogue and prices are pretty much the same as Amazon.in's, so it's probably the same imports from the same distributors.

  • Calcutta Records: a Kolkata store with a huge vinyl catalogue and a CD section, new and pre-owned, that ships across India. The catch is the prices. Plenty of their CDs are priced above ₹4,000, which is what you'd pay for a record and defeats the whole point of buying CDs. Some are closer to ₹2,000, which is at least more reasonable.

  • Amazon.in: mostly imports at import prices (though some amazing, more sensible picks at around Jakarta prices), plus a few Indian film CDs from sellers of varying reliability.

  • Discogs: has practically everything, but comes with international shipping and customs roulette.
  • Secondhand: thrift shops, OLX, and the odd lot on eBay. Cheap if you get lucky, but you have to keep looking.

It works, sort of, if you're patient and willing to hunt. But there's no browsing. There's no walking into a shop and walking out with five discs you didn't plan on buying. The discovery part of physical media, which is half the point, is just missing.

Importing personally can't save you in this case, and it's worse for CDs than it is for vinyl. If I want to import a record, it's roughly ₹2,500 for the music, up to ₹2,000 for shipping, and up to ₹1,000 in customs. That's steep, but the shipping is a fraction of what you're paying for. Shipping a CD costs about the same, but the disc itself is only about ₹1,500. Add roughly 30% in duty for personal imports, and a ₹1,500 CD costs around ₹4,000 by the time it reaches you, about the same as a new LP here.

Vinyl buyers here have it better. Record stores like The Revolver Club and On The Jungle Floor (which only sells vinyl) will source an LP they don't have in stock, and sell it to you at the same price as the ones on their shelves. They can do that because enough people buy records here that their distributors bring them in routinely. Nobody does that for CDs, because nobody's buying them, so every CD that isn't already in the country has to contend with the shipping and customs arithmetic above. They also have gorgeous stores where you can dig through crates and talk to the folks working there and get exposed to new music.

Labels don't press CDs in India anymore either. Sony used to run a disc plant in Mumbai that pressed Bollywood soundtracks like Barfi!, and it shut down in 2016. The capacity to press CDs probably still exists in India, with plenty of businesses offering to make discs. Labels just don't use it, because there's barely a market to sell to. So every new release on sale here is an import, and can never be sold for under ₹500, which is what I think a new CD should cost here, given what Americans and Europeans pay and the difference in cost of living.

Indian indie bands could get a few hundred CDs made here without spending much, but there are no record stores to stock them and almost nobody with a CD player to buy them. So most bands skip the format and go straight to streaming, or to vinyl if they can afford it.

Peter Cat Recording Co. self-released their first album on CD in India in 2011. By Bismillah in 2019, the only CD was from their French label, and every vinyl press of it has been made in Germany. Their 2024 album Beta came out on vinyl only, through an American label. One of India's best-known indie bands sells its music back to Indian fans as imported vinyl, and doesn't sell CDs at all.

That market is something I want to help build. I'd like to be able to buy a new album for ₹500, the way people elsewhere can. And I want them back in physical stores, too. Like I found in Jakarta, seeing a CD on a shelf is half of what makes you want it. If enough of us are buying, labels have a reason to press locally, and a new album on CD becomes a ₹500 impulse buy instead of a ₹4,000 import.

A brief word from the Discman propaganda department

CD players are cheap. A working used Discman costs less than a single new LP in India. I got one, and it plays CD-Rs just fine, which means mixtapes are back on the menu. Eighty minutes of algorithm-free listening, on hardware older than my interns.

Mine was purchased on Circle, but as of the time of writing, they don’t have any in stock.

Even many fancy new ones on hi-fi shops like the Headphone Zone are cheaper than the cheapest turntables they have in stock.

The timing is weirdly right

CD revenue in the US grew 58.6% in the first half of 2026 compared to the year before, driven largely by K-pop and physical media as merch. India's first CD era barely got going before it was over, but the second one doesn't have to go the same way.

Let's do something about it

I can't fix import duties, but some of this is fixable if there are enough of us.

So I'm starting a community for Indian CD people. Somewhere to post finds and map out where the good secondhand stores are. Mostly, though, it's for group orders. Shipping is what kills an imported CD, and it doesn't care how many discs are in the box. Split one shipment ten ways and that ₹4,000 CD starts looking more like ₹2,000.

If any of this resonated, come join the WhatsApp community.

And one more thing, because I can't help myself. The Discmans we're all buying secondhand won't last forever, and nobody makes a good, affordable CD player anymore. If it turns out there are enough of us, I would love to work on an open-hardware one. Consider this post the demand survey.

entry.title: What the Pho, Rosh? - #8
entry.content:
My Vietnam travelogue series is fondly named WTP, Rosh. You can read part 7 here, and all the previous posts in this series here.

Despite having lost the rest of Walking Tour crew, I wasn’t ready to give up yet. I stood in the middle of the lobby of that fancy mall and tried calling the number listed in the walking tour invitation. No answer.

I tried again. Same.

I thought I’d try one last time, and this time the voices in my head answered.

They apparently tuned me in as a spectator on a conference call they were having.

Inner Critic: I cannot believe we’re doing this again! Wasn’t our experience in Germany really not enough to learn from? This is the THIRD TIME we’re getting left behind on a walking tour! She needs an intervention at this point.

Chindi-ness with a resolve: But we can’t leave the walking tour NOW! We paid good money for it and we will make the most of it!!

Anxiety: What are even you talking about? We don’t know where the walking tour has gone, forget making the most of it. What we should “make the most of” is our common sense and book a pho-kin ride home.

Weird-voice-masked-as-gratefulness: You know it’s so easy to spot a lost tourist! We should be grateful we are not “taken” yet!

Anxiety & Embarrassment in chorus: AAAHHHHHHHH

PING!! My Grab ride back to the Airbnb was confirmed. 

Sarcasm: **rolls eyes while filing her nails** So much for labelling yourself persistent.

I checked out of this conference call and walked towards the pick up point. I found my Grab driver and raised my hand to wave at him when… 

Another PING!!

I had a notification on my Walking Tour chat on Airbnb! The host had sent me the current location they were at and it was a two minute walk (run) from where I was.

I put my hand down before the Grab driver saw me and cancelled the ride (I am sorry kind sir!). Then, I yeeted towards that location. Powered by Google maps and the recent trail run victory.

Once I reached the location, I saw everyone with a popsicle. Why did this make it to the walking tour?

Turns out it was an old, ice cream shop in Hanoi from the 1950s and I honestly don’t remember the rest of the details. But what I do remember was that it had vegan ice cream options! :D

“Joy” entered the conference call with just as much drama as the rest of the crew while I got myself a nice vegan popsicle.

What was so special about the walking tour that this whole incident of 20 minutes had to be dramatized? Well, let’s say it’s a little bit about closure to events, a little bit about self-confidence, and a LOT about silencing the voices in my head. 

Sweet lord, a popsicle was simply the perfect way to silence them!

entry.title: Hamilton
entry.content:
Dear Hiya,

You ask me to write about a book that influenced me. Alexander Hamilton by Ron Chernow was appealing to me, beyond the fact that all biographies are appealing to sixteen-year-olds, because it suggested that it was possible to have a rich intellectual life that is also a life of action.

Consider the image of Hamilton, first as an artillery captain and then on Washington’s staff in his early twenties, writing reports on army reorganisation and returning at night to make notes in which he “recorded tables from Postlethwayt[’s Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce] showing infant-mortality rates, population growth, foreign-exchange rates, trade balances, and the total economic output of assorted nations.” Consider also how prolific he was in the midst of all this, and how contemporaries wondered how one man wrote so much. Consider how he was a competent executive as Treasury Secretary, and a progenitor of the architecture of the American federal government.

I remember, after reading Chernow, wanting to understand the world as well as act in it. It was nice, as a teenager, to imagine that while we work in the midst of great historical forces, individuals do matter; the choices we make may not only lash against the shores but, from day to day, may shift the tides.

There’s a similar combination of action and thought in the life of Keynes, who is remembered, like Hamilton, for his essential liberalism and his faith in the project of what they thought of as civilisation. Keynes’s line about “[m]admen in authority” distilling their frenzy from “some academic scribbler” has offered, for better or for worse, comfort to many public policy professionals.

Yours sincerely,
Nihal

entry.title: Wishful Arguments Against Ai
entry.content:
Some arguments against AI are really important to consider. Others are simply non-sequitors that pile on

AI is not intelligent

AI is intelligent enough to be called intelligent. It gives answers and solves problems, on average better than an idiotic human being. (And even an idiotic human being will be considered to be possessing “intelligence”, although the measure of that in arbitrary tests like “IQ” will be less.)

Being right all the time is not called “intelligence” it is called “omniscience”. It is not AO, it is AI.

So, AI can be wrong, and that doesn’t disqualify it from being called AI.

AI destroys independent web

Without data, this doesn’t mean much. AI helps people set up websites independently. So, AI creates independent web too.

I have been running several websites (including this blog) on the smallest VPS of hetzner. Even before AI, and even after AI. The server runs a mediawiki instance, 8 wordpress instances, 15+ static sites, and a couple of other database intensive services.

In the beginning, with content scraping, the php-fpm used to get choked. But with some tweaks in configuration (increasing workers, setting up cache on wordpress and preventing access to history/diff for non-logged-in users on mediawiki) and switching some sites to frankenphp, I’ve not had any issue. I never had to use cloudflare or anubis or captcha or anything to keep the sites live.

Violation of copyright

I do not believe that copyright is an inviolable principle. There is indeed inequity in who is able to violate copyright without consequences. It is completely unfair that models are being kept as “proprietary” and it would be completely fair to free such models from the gatekeepers and release them for anyone to use.

Destroying rare physical books

It is wrong to destroy books, especially if they’re rare.

Exploitation of workers

It is wrong to exploit humans. And there’s all kinds of exploitation going on in all kinds of labor sectors.

Exploitation of nature

It is wrong to exploit nature for greed. And there’s all kinds of such exploitation going on.

Privacy

The choice of how much privacy is needed should always be left to individuals.

Deskilling

Deskilling happens because of misuse. It is possible to increase skills using AI, if used to that end. And vice versa.

Burnout of free software maintainers

Only popular projects get overwhelmed by AI. There is a long tail of free software projects where AI is decreasing developer effort and prevents burnout.

Layoffs

AI indeed creates existential questions to humankind. What’s the purpose of labor if everything gets automated? Capitalism needs to be uprooted. What to do about bullshit jobs, though? Humans shouldn’t have to do meaningless jobs.

Weakening democracies

Human beings being gullible and un-intelligent is the original weakness of democracies.

and a lot of other things…

It’s all true.

But it’s all true about the rest of the world also.

We live in a messy, problematic, risky, dirty world.

Do I use AI?

I don’t use AI when writing things. I don’t read AI written articles (and I can say in a few sentences).

When coding, I use AI in some situations (tedious migrations, prototyping frontends, bugfixes).

When using software written by others, I judge based on whether it solves my problems or not. If the use is going to long-term, I judge whether a software project is going to survive long term based on various parameters (including whether the author can code without AI).

I use AI answers (like Gemini) in a wide variety of situations: brainstorming best practices; discovering books, websites, articles, guidelines; quickly quenching curiosities; finding way forward when I’m stuck; etc. I use &udm=14 to avoid google showing AI answers without me asking for it.

entry.title: The Tree and the Girl
entry.content:
Posted on Jan 30, 2022.

A tree grew in between the road. The road morphed around the tree like rivers around mountains. Alongside the road was a garden, and the other side was lined with houses.

The girl I loved stayed near the tree, so near as to become a part of the tree. I wondered how she could stay close to the tree when the road was often flooded with unflinching traffic. The girl had dark curly hair, and light bounced off her creamy earthen-skin, it made her shine during the day and twinkle at night. But she never was away from the tree.

I came to know of her whenever I traveled this patch of the road or came for a stroll in the park. Her face magnetized me. She looked like a wooden carving of a goddess of nature itself.

I loved the calmness of her face and the defiant way she stood on the road while the whole world moved passed her in a rush of meaningless existence. Her presence always compelled me to take this road no matter where I went.

For the past several weeks, she kept emerging in my dreams. That’s where I had fallen in love with her. In dreams, we sat legs dandling, on a tree branch where birds surrounded her, enamored by her voice. Then she looked at me, smiled and whispered "I love you as nature loves her creations". I touched her hand and said that I love her too. Then we roamed like wind through the garden, the road, the houses, and then reaching far north towards the ocean, but the wind carrying the fresh air from the sea awoke me.

That day I hurried to look at her, and when I reached the road I saw her standing by the tree. I always saw her standing near the tree, and the times I did not, my heart ached. Imagining her anyplace far away from the tree, without me, pained me. That thought all but cornered me to walk towards her.

I walked across the road, looking around as to avoid getting crushed by the onslaught of traffic. Each step I took to be near her was exhilarating. When I reached her, her gaze was transfixed at something afar, still I said ”Hi, I saw you in my dreams. I’m in love with you. And, you love me too, in those dreams.”

Her gazed didn’t flinched, so I continued “There’s always a ton of traffic going by on this road. It’s dangerous being near this tree. Doesn’t the air smell stal?”

I stopped for a response, but she said nothing.

“Listen, don’t your legs hurt standing here? The tree doesn’t have any branches to sit on as well. Did you plant it here, are you it’s mother? I like nature you know, I love walks in the parks, birds, and you.”

She stood there as still as the tree. This made my chest stop, I started breathing heavily.

“I mean if you like to stay here. It is your choice. But be careful. Also, I see you every day, have you seen me around? I often walk around here or travel by this road. I always see you. You must recognize my face?” I got my face right in front of her.

She finally looked at me and smiled. Her eyes directed me to her hands, they were tightly closed but she opened them like blooming flowers. It excited me to see what was she holding but when the flower fully bloomed it was empty.

I only saw her palm, birth lines running up and down on her curved hand. I wanted to hold it, feel it, and never let it go.

So I grabbed hold of her hand and said “They have everything over there like anything you can think of I will buy it for you. It will only take a moment, and you can come back whenever you feel like it.”

She shook her head, broke her hand apart from mine and resumed the wondering gaze towards something I could not fathom.

Her stillness finally broke me, it discouraged my windpipe to open anymore and hurt my chest like shards of broken glass. The flood of traffic around us had cleared, so I said “I don’t like this tree, it creates traffic on the road. They should cut it down,” and left.

I went home for the day. My mind kept replaying the stillness of her face over each word I had said. I was helpless but to reimagine the torture. I could not decide why she had not moved from there.

That night I just stared into the darkness, until my eyes closed. Then I saw her smiling face. Now she was talking with me. We talked a lot, and we were far away from the tree. The wind carried the smell of the sea, sand was beneath our feet, and my hands were wrapped around hers. She had soft hands, I held them tightly.

We were standing on the shore, in front of our eyes the ocean stretched to the horizon and beyond. Looking at her smile swayed my worries afar. Then with delight, she directed me to look at something behind me. I turned around, and I saw a tree emerging from beneath the ocean. The waves came and went, but the tree stood tall, afloat on the water, untouched.

Then I saw my love plunge into the ocean towards the tree. I was terrified and haunted all at once. She did not care for the waves that pushed her. The waves crashed into her, pushing her ashore, but she stood up again and broke through the oncoming wall of water. She looked majestic standing waist-high in the ocean. She swam farther and farther into the water until only the back of her head was visible, but the tree was still beyond her reach. Seeing this I shouted “It’s too far away! You will never reach it. Come back to me!”

The waves kept crashing into her relentlessly, but she kept emerging again and again. She was still far away from the tree when a huge wave came and washed over her, making her disappear. I kept waiting and waiting for her to emerge through it, to see her again. But, on the surface of the vast ocean, only the waves and the tree remained.

When I awoke there were tears in my eyes. In that instance, I had decided something. I walked out at night into the darkness with one hand holding an axe. When I reached the fated road it was wrapped in darkness. The sky was devoid of moonlight, nor the streetlights shone. But I could still see the silhouette of the tree with its to long twisted branches haunting the middle of the road.

I started to swing the axe at its roots. The hacking was devoid of any rhythm or reason, just pure rage. Then my body fell into the motion of hacking the tree like the clicking of the clock. I'm unaware of how long it took to axe the tree to death. I stood there with my whole being aching by the time the road was devoid of any life. I left the axe on the side of the road, and step out of the darkness leaving the road far behind.

That night I slept again, this time cradled in the arms of darkness. When I awoke, the sun had risen to its peak, and my body felt numb to pain or emotions. I followed my first instinct to see her. When I arrived on the road, I imagined her befuddled or broken down into tears or in deep mourning. But I only found the road busy with traffic as usual, but only now, it did not morph around the tree.

entry.title: Grand Challenges Now, Gloom (Maybe) Later
entry.content:
Dear Calvin,

Yesterday, I wrote to you about how I’m keeping the LLM gloom at bay. Here’s what I think will happen: humankind will have to navigate a grand transition; it will require all our effort and all our intelligence (and all the LLMs we can leverage). The idea of superintelligence (as some sort of alien power with the capacity to subjugate) has not gripped me. Existential risk from AI isn’t what keeps me up at night. Instead, I have more boring worries: I imagine enormous industries will be upended, and many people will be out of work.

A sense of alienation is normal under these circumstances. For those of us who have very prized, previously scarce, high-value intellectual work, at least some of what is lost is the sense that we mattered, that there were problems that only we could solve. With cheap, indefatigable intelligence as the baseline, that outsized marginal impact is much diminished—we are concerned that we are less likely to make our mark on the world, on our times.

In 1841, Lincoln was about 31 years old. He had not yet become President, assembled a cabinet of his rivals, overseen the deaths of three-quarters of a million men in the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, or pushed the Thirteenth Amendment through Congress. He was deeply depressed. His friends, worried that he might commit suicide, removed razors and other sharp objects from his rooms. Lincoln wrote to John T. Stuart, his law partner:

I am now the most miserable man living. If what I feel were equally distributed to the whole human family, there would not be one cheerful face on the earth. Whether I shall ever be better I can not tell; I awfully forebode I shall not. To remain as I am is impossible; I must die or be better, it appears to me.

During this period of suicidal ideation, according to his friend Joshua Speed, what kept Lincoln going was a sense that he had ‘done nothing to make any human being remember that he had lived,’ and a wish to ‘connect his name with the events transpiring in his day and generation, and so impress himself upon them as to link his name with something that would redound to the interest of his fellow man.’ This, as Speed put it, was what he desired to live for.

What’s my p(gloom), you ask? I think the Civil War was an immensely gloomy time. But we will have no shortage of opportunities to serve the interests of our fellow humans. If that is worth living for, then, amidst the gloom, we have plenty to live for. We have to think about how the world will change and help people adapt when it does. This is also what drove me to public policy: the intractable problems all around me, crying out for a lever. Well, here we are, with the longest lever ever built, getting longer every day, and a world about to move.

In fact, we will be drowning in work. Concretely, we will have to figure out how to pace the frontier, if that is what we must do. We will have to find work or support for the hundreds of millions who will be made redundant by new technology. We will have to navigate the social upheavals that result, and care for our loved ones. In much of the developing world, we will have to achieve high economic growth without being at the frontier of these technologies, and apply the technologies to improve public services and living standards. We will have to build alliances and likely fight wars.

Death, in the form of John Wilkes Booth, did eventually come for Lincoln. But it came in 1865, twenty-four years after Lincoln’s depressive episode. Maybe superintelligence will come for us too. Even so, it’s much better to take the risk of John Wilkes Booth than to end it all in 1841. Well, maybe we’re in 1843. But put the razors away. There’s work to do.

Yours sincerely,
Nihal

entry.title: Pose page has been reworked
entry.content:
The page you are looking at is reworked to have weekly grouping, although I strictly want to post small bits everyday like Mastodon posts. The only friction I feel with Mastodon is that like any other social media it still has that "Feedback Craving": when I post, I keep expecting someone to star it and reply. The constant tension of someone overlooking it might demotivate me from writing anything more. Thus here I'm writing on my own site without caring for anything, but whatever it is, this holds as a document for myself to see over the "world wide web". No reaction craving, nor any self-pitfalls.

I should write about my hate towards the reaction system altogether as a blog post, and I should find a way to hide them everywhere. I know it's very useful, but I totally hate it. At least a respectful way to hide them, as a user preference, would help. YouTube did it, but on their end; I'd prefer it on the user (client) end.
