entry.title: I Write Club (IWC) - Chapter Two
entry.content:
Jacqualeen said, "Now that the writing session is over. Let's begin today's discussion: Why write?"

Someone sitting on the first bench raised their hand and said, "I'm good at writing. I've won awards for writing essays in school which encouraged me to write more. Now I run the college's monthly newspaper for which I do research and write." 

Jacqualeen said, "That's wonderful, Sebastian! Newspapers have to publish stuff everyday. They can't simply stop writing!"  

Someone pitched in, "Of course! Writing is how the world works. It's all papers, affidavits, pamphlets, certificates! If we stop writing, the world stops working!" 

An old man, seated on the 2nd desk, said, "I started writing 40 years ago, on my Remington Typewriter. I wrote letters and poems to my dear love. Now she has passed away, but I still keep writing letters and poems to her, to tell her how much I love her." He chuckled after saying that. 

Jacqualeen said, "Rupert, you're a true romantic!" 

Then feeling a lull in the room I said, "I don't write, but I want to start writing to tell stories that are interesting to me."

Everyone turned to look at me. 

Jacqualeen said, "Yes. It's a gift you must share with the world, and us. You will be writing a lot from now on. I look forward to the stories you'll tell." 

"Um...sure." 

Then a girl sitting in the front said, "I love reading romance books which encouraged me to write romance stories myself. I publish them to my site. It's S----, feel free to check it out!"

After that a few more people shared why they write, then the conversation moved on to what stops us from writing. 

Someone said, "A weak resolve!" Another said, "laziness!", "Procrastination!"

Someone said, "My wife!"  Everyone laughed.

Then the person, Gerald, who has asked a question about membership earlier said, "I don't have time to write. It's hard to focus, and I get distracted easily. Also, I don't know what to write, and when I do know what I want to write then the words are hard to come by. Maybe, I'm not meant to write?"

"Gerald, you're new to IWC. We all come here with such doubts or excuses. But, let me tell you something. There's only one thing that stops us from writing... a demon" She paused, looked around the room, then said "A demon within us. It creates such self doubt, excuses, tries to smother your fire. But, will you let it smother your gift, or will you burn the demon with your fire?"

Gerald said, "I would like to... burn the demon?"

She said, "May you have the Goddess blessing then, let the demon burn away or burn with the demon!"

Most of the people sitting in the front desks murmured something that to me seemed like a prayer. 

Then I decided to asked a question myself, "But, how do I know if writing is my calling? We all have the ability to write but why should I write?"

She smiled and said, "It's cause you stand here. Asking this question that proves that it's your calling!"

"But, I stand in doubt. I'm not sure if this is the correct place for me."

"I read your story. It's wonderful. I believe in you. The goddess believes in you."

"uhhmm... thanks"

I felt speechless, so I sat down. After that there were some more discussions around writers block; how to overcome it, and being accountable. Then the session part of the meetup was over and people started to mingle and talked with each other.

I joined a nearby group to hear the discussion. 

"Yesterday, I wrote after waking up, then during my commute, after lunch, and before bed. On my working days I follow this schedule, otherwise..."

I moved to the next group of people.

"...feeds the goddess of knowledge. Thoughts have so much power, but when written down they bring energy and life to this world" Said a girl, she had a scarf on her head, and a peacock necklace. She was talking with three others. She said, "You know, I don't read other people's writing, you never know what energy will jump out of those pages and consume you. It's too much for a my mental peace."

I moved close towards the front desks to see if I could find someone who speaks my wavelength. Before, I could approach another group I felt someone's hand on my shoulder. I looked around to see the same guy, Gerald, who asked the question, "what happens if full members don't write". 

He smiled and said, "Hi, I see you're like me. It's also your first time here?"

I laughed and said, "Yes, nice questions that you asked earlier."

He said, "I guess, we will get to know in two months time. If you make it that long." He laughed and said, "Just merry making, for me writing even 2000 words per week is tough, so not so sure about myself."

I told him, "It would be fine. Simply burn the demon away!" Then we both laughed.

"Btw, I'm Ash and you?"

He extended his hand and said, "I'm Gerald, nice to meet you!".

We talked some more, Gerald is a department manager for a fast food franchise. However, he loves writing poems and journals. But, his life and job got in the way of writing these past few years. Recently, he decided to reconnect with it and somehow found out about this club. He also shared with me a short poem he wrote during the writing session. 

Times passes like words uttered to wind
You can never recall the whole, just a few pieces here and there
the rest forgotten as it never was, like it never lived
A dream of few words, fading in the wind

I could only say, "That's beautiful."

While we were talking, a young looking person stood near us, listening. Then he introduced himself.

"Hi, I'm Ray, I'm seeing both of you for the first time. Welcome to the club."

I replied, "Thanks, I'm Ash and this is Gerald" 

Gerald asked him, "Ray, are you a full member here?"

Ray said, "No, I'm a new member like you guys, but I'll become a full member next week."

We three talked for sometime and Gerald and I had a lot of questions to ask and were glad to find someone like us to have them answered. Ray had been writing consistently and attending these IWC meetings. He didn't know the rules of full membership, only as much as we knew. He writes a lot about all things, and also runs his university newspaper.

He said that everyone here is supportive and helpful and always encourages him to write more. They even checkup on him, so meeting the 2000 words per week goal isn't a problem. However, he said that he is a perfectionist and needs to always improve his writing, so it does take him a lot of time to write to his satisfaction. More people joined with him but none made it this long.  

I asked Ray, "What do you think makes someone stick out the 2 months and even continue being a member of this club? Writing everyday is not easy. Since you're coming here regularly what's so special about this club?"

He looked at me and thought for a few seconds before answering.

"I'm not sure, but after joining this club, writing feels different, more rewarding somehow. I feel the the more I write the more I change. I think better, I write better, and I feel great. It's almost like taking a medicine for a disease I didn't know I had, and now I'm finally recovering."

Gerald laughed, "So not writing is a disease?"

I pitched in, "It's an interesting way to describe it though. But, it seems like this club does help people write more."

He replied, "Yes, everyone here writes without fail." 

To me Ray seemed like a good kid. But, at the time, I couldn't help but feel something seemed off about this whole club. Unfortunately, I ignored the thought believing that I'll be encouraged, pressured, and motivated to write. What more could I ask for. So, I didn't overthink the minor stuff, only to regret it later. 

I let Gerald and Ray talk, and move on to another group, to see what more I could learn. I walked towards the group Jacqualeen was in. 

"Yes, you can publish a book about your daily life. Name it 365 days in grace." Said a guy.  

Someone replied, "That might not be interesting enough. But, I like the idea of writing everyday and making a book out of it." Then they saw me listening in, and the guy who replied said, "Hi Ash. What do you think about turning journals into a book?"

I said, "That sounds interesting. But, I don't write daily journals." 

Everyone standing in the group went silent then looked at me. Their gaze piercing my soul. The guy replied, "Welcome to the I Write Club, you'll be writing everyday here. Until the leave of course." Then he laughed, "But we won't let that happen to you. We would like to see you living out your calling till the very end. What's a man and a life, if he isn't living to his fullest, yeah?"

I smiled and agreed, then I asked. "How long have you been a member of this club? 

He said. "2 years, and everyone here has been a member for a few years. Let me introduce you to everyone. Starting with myself, I'm Samuel, here's Jordan, then you've already met Jacqualeen, and this is Nat." 

I said, "Hey everyone, I'm Ash. Nice to meet you all."

Nat asked, "So Ash, how do you felt during the writing session?"

"It was good, I was able to write a story I had thought of some months ago but never put it down on paper. Frankly, I found myself able to focus clearly, otherwise; I struggle with writing at home or office."

Nat said, "Do you know why you could focus today?"

"Not sure, but must be this environment and the spontaneity of it."

Nat said, "There is something special about this place, and the I Write Club, that helps it's members write more. Will you be happy if you completed your story?"

'Yes, if I reach that point."

Nat said, "Why won't you? You simply have to do what you did today, everyday. And, there's a whole community to help you or... punish you."

Samuel said, "Do you know the famous author R-----?"

I said, "Yes, I've read her books:"

Samuel replied, "She is member of the IWC" 

"Wow, really! I would love to meet her."

"Oh, you will, in due time"

It was then I had decided to join IWC. I wish I hadn't but then I was already trapped like a fly on the spiders web, the movement I walked into that room that day, or maybe even before that. 

After the meetup, I went home and life move on as usual until I got a letter from IWC.

Thanks for reading and it you would like to share comments, feedback, or advice please feel free to use this google form.

entry.title: Can we avoid land-grabs on the Moon through physics and geology instead of politics?
entry.content:
Last year, Intuitive Machines attempted to soft-land its Athena spacecraft on the Moon’s south pole at about 85° latitude as part of NASA’s CLPS program. China’s Chang’e 7 lander will launch next year to explore the south pole near Shackleton crater at ~89°S. By 2029, Chang’e 8 will also target a landing somewhere between 85°S to 89°S. Moreover, the exploration areas for the upcoming Indo-Japanese LUPEX rover mission lie around 89°S as well. And within a few degrees of it are targeted sites for several landers from Blue Origin, Europe’s MAGPIE rover mission, and some CLPS missions. Landing site candidates for NASA’s crewed Artemis IV mission so far also range in 85–89°S. Against the expanse of the Moon, the high south pole is a small region for countries globally to target.

All these missions have broad goals in common: locate, map, and analyze water ice deposits on or beneath the surface, and assess its potential use in future habitats to provide drinking water, breathable oxygen, or even rocket fuel. While time will thinly separate many of these missions for now, the next wave of Mooncraft will operate for longer and overlap more. If and when substantial lunar water deposits are identified, missions will further cluster in those places. It will create coordination & legal challenges, depletion of a natural & scientific resource, and potential conflicts among mission owners.

Gaps in governance and geopolitics

Earlier this year NASA JPL awarded a $75 million contract to Firefly to have its Elytra Dark spacecraft deliver 3-4 “Moonfall” hopper drones to low lunar orbit in 2028. From this orbit, each hopper will land on the Moon by itself. Each will study the lunar surface during hops with a few instruments. During this process, NASA aims to acquire lunar surface imagery with centimeter-level resolution ahead of crewed Artemis missions. Post-hops, NASA will use the resting positions of the drones to establish a Moonbase “perimeter”, intended to act as a “safety zone” under the US-led Artemis Accords convention. 

Open questions remain about such zoning on the Moon. How do lunar operators coordinate? How long do these effective no-go zones for others last? How is their spatial span defined? What if future mining operations in such regions make it difficult or virtually impossible for others to conduct their activities nearby either due to local dust kickup or political keep-out areas? How should we go about having shared or negotiated resource areas and mining limits on the Moon? How do we even agree on common rules in practice? The international Outer Space Treaty does forbid territorial appropriation of the Moon by countries but does not clarify practices at local scales. Made in the 1960s to cater to different needs, it’s not specific enough for the range of advanced missions expected in the 21st century by a more diverse set of operators—including commercial ones.

Space agencies and organizations globally, including commercial actors, thus recognize the impending need for a governance framework; codes of conduct for how we should operate collectively at our Moon. But the US and China are leading separate international cooperation efforts vis-à-vis the Artemis Accords and the ILRS Moonbase project respectively, with barely any signatories in common (Thailand is one, and tries to convene both sides). In 2024, China presented their thinking on the legal use of lunar resources at the United Nations, a positive development for potential mutual dialogue at an international fora, but one which also further contrasted the country’s stance with the non-binding nature of the Accords. Moreover, the US’ Wolf Amendment prevents NASA and other government-funded organizations from meaningfully collaborating with China on any missions. Christine Tiballi, a former researcher and project lead with Open Lunar, highlighted one such challenge in the Lunar Compass:

Despite the parallel focus on standards, cooperation, and interoperability, neither the Accords nor ILRS explicitly states its objectives in relation to [territorial] non-appropriation (permanence), nor its willingness to cooperate (beyond due regard) with the other, setting the stage for terrestrial geopolitical conflict to remain tethered to us.

Amid these disparities and gaps in international laws, how do we sustainably explore our Moon? Even within a given bloc and its framework, will competing entities adhere to rules equally? Any one operator setting top-down governance norms for all can disincentivize the others from adopting mutual-benefit practices.

Piloting a pathway based on physics and practicality

Lunar hardware operators should be incentivized to adopt tools that aid their coordination with others while reducing mutual costs. It’s to this end that the Open Lunar Foundation (a Moon Monday sponsor) decided to develop what they call transparent, practical tools based on physics and geology instead of politics, in line with the non-profit’s stated mission to enable and promote cooperative, peaceful, and sustainable lunar exploration by all countries.

Open Lunar Fellow Aaron Mackey has developed a physics-based, open source If/Then Toolkit for operators. In version 1, it lets the operators transparently define required operational radii for safely conducting various lunar activities in their missions, such as the extent of dust kickup from drilling. The parameters get refined or verified with time based on data from accomplished missions. Adopting such a tool & method would avoid de facto operator claims over arbitrarily large lunar areas while also helping their missions secure minimum viable areas for safe operations anchored in physics not politics. Vic Paulson, another Open Lunar Fellow, has developed Overlap, an also-open-source tool; this one specifically for future lunar operators to do policy simulations. In the first release of the Overlap governance game based on real lunar south polar data, operators conduct mission activities in parallel, which exposes operational overlaps between them. As operators try to meet their goals while maneuvering around possible conflicts, the outcomes surface the harmful consequences of various policy choices while real hardware is still on Earth. Actual future missions can then fly with safer operational plans.

These works build upon Tiballi’s proposed three-ring structure around mission hardware for operators to peacefully coordinate with each other. In this structure, the innermost core ring is exclusive to the hardware owner & operator while their middle ring can be entered by another operator after seeking permission. The outermost ring can be entered and traversed through by others without permission but with a notification. Mackey’s work defines the sizes of the three rings based on the physics of respective activities and Paulson’s work anchors the operator interactions and their incentives in the geology of the Moon’s south pole.

These are not the only proposed solutions to the problem of lunar governance. People worldwide have considered utilizing existing governance treaties or frameworks such as UNCLOS, the Antarctic Treaty, UNFSA, ITU-R, and so on as these are being successfully used to manage shared resources on Earth. However, the reason for Mackey and Paulson’s works is that the basis for every single one of these existing treaties does not hold at the Moon and its south pole, which is a completely different natural environment than anything we’ve seen on Earth. Paulson noted:

Every proposed lunar governance framework borrows from Earth. Each encodes hard-won lessons about managing shared resources without sovereignty. And each of them breaks down when it is applied to the lunar south pole. Lunar water ice is finite, geographically fixed, and non-renewable on any human timescale. No existing framework was built with that in mind.

As such, while a lunar coordination framework can borrow relevant elements from existing international mechanisms, it also needs to account for, from scratch, the non-renewability of polar water ice and other volatiles as well as their limited access corridors. Given that the geography and geology of the Moon’s south pole naturally limits the grouping of favorable areas for different kinds of mission needs, operational overlap even among mutually well-meaning actors is inevitable. What Mackey and Paulson’s tools thus aim for is practical coordination between operators that can surface conflicts in advance to hopefully effectively resolve or manage them on real missions.

Sharing the south pole for self help

It may seem at first that relying on operators to adopt governance tools is a naive proposition. That one can simply ignore the ringed areas defined and declared by another operator to access valuable resources. But one should also factor in the reality that the poles are the harshest regions of the Moon to operate in. Moreover, many past space and Moon missions have shown that operational errors do terminate missions or severely degrade outcomes. Making it to the Moon in one piece is hard enough; half the recent attempts globally have failed. Grabbing success at the lunar south pole only adds to the challenges. Total lack of information sharing and coordination between missions would neither be safe nor efficient for progress. As such, every operator will want to avoid losing multi-hundred-million-dollar hardware, especially from jagged lunar dust being thrown around by operations of other missions. Operators have at least a baseline incentive to coordinate missions, and to share and even buy data, so as to reduce their own risks and costs.

Mackey’s Toolkit allows defining & visualizing operational and coordination areas for active lunar hardware based on the physics of its activities and true outcomes. In turn, the real parameters help calibrate and refine assessments for future zones. Such operator-agnostic transparency is intended not only so that they don’t inadvertently harm each other but also because any operator’s operational control over an area should only be as large or small as the physics really requires. This is how we can go about collectively characterizing a wide range of operational hazards such as dust kickup from nearby landings or mining operations, electromagnetic interference from power or communications towers, radiation from nuclear sources, and so on. Mackey noted:

The goal is to incentivize operators to resolve conflicts before they become crises, and to build the kind of structured self-coordination that makes future conflict less likely. The tool is flexible and adaptable so specialists can input and verify the right units and scales.

Most importantly, each three-ring structure is meant to cease with the mission or its specific operations. The Toolkit aims to provide operators a way to protect and self-regulate their lunar operations without permanently owning the lunar land itself. “They only claim operational control of a specific activity in a specific zone and for a specific time, substituting sovereignty claims for operational coordination that fits squarely within the bounds of the Outer Space Treaty,” added Mackey.

Overcoming operational overlaps

As Moon missions become more complex over time, the Toolkit is meant to evolve with them. As simple, infrequent operational overlaps at the edges transition to denser, multi-actor overlaps, the Toolkit’s past deployments will not only help determine true, physics-based boundaries but help refine operational practices amid inevitable disparities. If we have past mission coordination details & outcomes published among operators through independent entities, such as the Lunar Ledger by Open Lunar (a Moon Monday sponsor) or any such equivalent portals (but which don’t exist yet), it will help the safety and success of everyone in one of the harshest environments in the Solar System.

The Toolkit can do one more thing: export a range of hypothetical-but-plausible activity from upcoming missions into Paulson’s simulation tool Overlap. As hardware density on the lunar south pole rises swiftly with time, it will become increasingly difficult for everyone to coordinate effectively if doing so only in real time—even when using things like the Toolkit. Paulson’s lunar surface & activities simulation tool based on real maps anticipates this problem and invites operators and countries to test governance methods, scenarios, strategies, and their likely outcomes. This can highlight core issues and their potential solutions while complex, expensive hardware is still on Earth.

Overlap’s high-fidelity to lunar geology tied to mission activities is intentional. In the policy game, two rival coalition programs compete and cooperate over water ice across terrain derived from the data of NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), particularly its instruments LOLA, LEND, Diviner, and LROC. Paulson explained the advantage of using real lunar data in Geology writes the rules:

A slope map or a temperature map describes what the surface is. A favorability map describes what the surface is good for. By weighting each layer according to what a mission phase actually needs and combining the layers into a single index, we turn a geology product into a planning product. The result is no longer a map an engineer has to translate. It is a map an engineer can read directly.

Negotiation during simulations happens at virtual tables on neutral lunar terrain, just like on Earth. The whole experience is a tactile way for actors and nations to test various tradeoffs before hardening any mission choices for optimal success. “Treaties have opinions, goals, and philosophies. But games produce competition, behavior, and human outcomes,” remarked Paulson to highlight the choice of policy gaming as an effective tool for the job.

Between increased data sharing by some operators and the availability of Toolkit and Overlap, we now have an initial set of grounded tools to incentivize and enable coordination between mission operators at the Moon. As missions evolve, the tools will need to as well. Adoption can provide the critical feedback necessary for adaptation. “The coordination infrastructure for Earth Orbit came too late, and now we're managing a crisis instead of preventing one,” noted Mackey.

With the Moon, we have a clean slate but only for a short period of time. It’s important we get it right. “Let’s fight physics instead of each other,” said Louis Burtz, whose team shared operations data from their YAOKI lunar rover on the Ledger earlier this year. The work that happens in this decade and next will set the precedents that shape lunar and deep space exploration for centuries.

Gifts galore!

Day: Nine
Date: 22 November, 2026

entry.title: Tell me why avoidance is not a good grief dealing strategy
entry.content:
I don’t know if this post is a story, an opinion, or a cry for help.

I don’t usually post things like this. Usually it’s conclusions to a series of thoughts. This time, I am smack-dab in the middle of those thoughts, and I am doing a conventionally recommended way of dealing with grief – writing about it.

Apparently, this method also works if you just write this as a letter and send it into the void. But that’s a level of vulnerability I’m’ not ready for yet. At least not today. Maybe next week.

I lost my friend M over five weeks ago. Three days after receiving this information - I gave myself four weeks to completely avoid thinking about it. I didn’t avoid it completely, but I avoided it a fair bit.

M did this of their own will. I’ve tried writing this sentence in a bunch of ways - but only this version makes me not bawl my eyes out.

I had known M for the better part of a decade. We weren’t very close, but we maintained an honest and consistent friendship. A couple days before their death, we hung out for an extended period of time. We hung out. M shared about life. Some setbacks, some pains. Some hopes, some aspirations – maybe ambitions. Some loss and some grief. I shared also shared some. Some platitudes, too. Promises were made to be more intentional and consistent in our connection.

I don’t understand why avoidance gets such a bad rep as a strategy for dealing with pain. I know the common wisdom - it’s not healing; it’s not moving through the pain and coming out the other side; it will come out in not-good ways; etc.

Dear reader – I have not been this productive in my entire fucking life.

When I first learned of M‘s death, it was without detail. Just that they were alive no more. The next couple of hours moved through loss, sadness, regret, consolation. Anger at them for being so careless. Rationalization to deal with this. From dust, to dust – haven’t you heard it?

I think I have now glimpsed a kind of pain whose existence horrified me. I don’t know how to deal with this. That is why - on Day 3 itself, I chose not to. I know that grief comes in waves. The waves must also get smaller with time, right? Maybe I can meet the waves when they are smaller.

I should have done better. I wish M had done better. I wish the world hadn’t convinced M to take this step. There’s perhaps a world where M is here and better, and perhaps that world was just one conversation away – I wish I was in that world. I wish I could have seen the pain.

The pooja was followed by having a lot of sweets and spending time with family… before the firecrackers began. After that, there were just explosions that went on past midnight. People setting off bombs to celebrate the festival of lights. ¶

I’m not going to tap into the anger from that day for my own peace of mind. But here’s what I left on my Instagram Stories on Diwali. ¶

“a pigeon has been trying to enter the house because it’s scared of the bombs, but it’ll be sad to know the sound isn’t any less louder inside.

a lot of animals are probably confused right now, because the temperature doesn’t feel right for hibernation. but they don’t know what AQI or climate change is.

our grandparents will be coughing and wheezing, and our parents will get headaches. your own dogs and cats will be scared as hell.

but hey look at you, you got to play with gunpowder and be a man today! how adorable.”

Later in the week, me and my sister got our ears pierced. Mine was a re-piercing after the last one didn’t go well, and she got a second piercing. I tried gaslighting her that the gunshot would hurt but she didn’t get baited. I might’ve already gotten karmic repercussions though, because mine did hurt slightly. ¶

I was going to add a picture of the piercings but turns out ears can act as unique identifiers? Human bodies are quite cool.

To quote myself from the last weeknote, “I’m at home sitting in a familiar chair, watching anime on a familiar TV. Life is good.” ¶

entry.title: p(gloom)
entry.content:
Dear Calvin,

You ask: I’d like to know what you currently feel about the current state of LLMs and the future they present to you/us. Basically, what is your p(gloom) status? Just describe your gloom if it exists.

Gloom hasn’t come for me yet, but Fernando is going through it after the Riemann proof:

Rand’s essay says: how great is Man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty! The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on.

One thing we must reject is self-importance. We have been causing misery, off to the side, decade after decade, automating away profession after profession. When I hear self-important pessimism of this kind, I feel like Jeremy Irons in Margin Call: ‘Jesus, when did you start feeling so sorry for yourself? It’s unbearable. What, you think we may have helped put some people out of business today? That it’s all just for naught? Well, you’ve been doing that every day for almost forty years, Sam.’ Our work feels miraculous and special and important to us. But we have automated away so much handicraft, so much miracle, so much specialness for consumer surplus, so that we may mass produce more goods, so there might be less poverty, and so that beauty would be more accessible.

I don’t mean to be unfeeling about this. I understand that this is painful, as I’m sure it will be painful for me one day. I saw a lot of mockery of sad mathematicians following Navier–Stokes, and now after the discovery of a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. ‘Do you want progress, or do you want to cosplay as intellectuals?’ seems to be the angle of attack. We must reject this philistine inhumanity comprehensively. The melancholic emotions—sadness, loss, suffering—are hard to relate to in the abstract. Suffering happens off to the side. In Musée des Beaux Arts, Auden describes Bruegel’s painting Landscape with the Fall of Icarus:

About suffering they were never wrong,
The old Masters: how well they understood
Its human position: how it takes place
While someone else is eating or opening a window or just walking dully along;

On the sidelines of every ‘miraculous birth’, there are ‘children who did not specially want it to happen, skating on a pond at the edge of the wood.’ We all deserve consolation. I hope people will be kind to me when my time comes, and I too am forced to change. The thing that keeps me from being gloomy, I suppose, is reciting the prayer of St Francis, and seeking ‘to comfort, rather than be comforted.’

Yours affectionately,
Nihal

entry.title: What the Pho, Rosh? - #7
entry.content:
My Vietnam travelogue series is fondly named WTP, Rosh. You can read all the previous posts in this series here.

“HAPPY BIRTHDAYYYY, ROSHNIIIIII!!”

The speakers boomed with the race announcer’s voice as I crossed the finish line of my first trail run.

“ROSHNI FROM INDIAAAA!”

He added.

What a way to celebrate my birthday, I thought to myself. I had planned for a breathtaking (and challenging) trail to run on and my partner to run with. But to be celebrated like that? In another country? With 4000+ runners on the course? 

After all that had happened?

Gosh! Vietnam doesn’t fail to surprise me - and this time for the better.

As they awarded me my finisher medal, I looked to my side to see M. “You’re glowing,” she remarked, beaming at me with pride. 

After some quality photoshoot, I video-called my mum who also observed the radiant glow I donned post the run, and smiled ear to ear as she did so.

A compliment? After a brief period of silent “disappointment”? 

That was her love letter / olive branch to me to say she was burying the hatchet and inviting me to do so. Of course I accepted the invitation. I’m not an idiot to carry resentment with me all the way to the mountains. 

But… I am somewhat of an idiot otherwise. 

You’d think that all these beautiful times in the mountains were the start of good times to come. Okay, you didn’t - but I did. 

Sigh.

Then again - What is the point of this series if not a safe space to recall and laugh at my follies? ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

M’s trip was short and we wanted to make the most of it - like any tourist on a budget and time crunch. On M’s last day in Vietnam, we decided to go for a 3 hour walking tour, which would end 2 hours prior to her flight. And the airport was 1 hour away from where we were.

Was it a big risk? Yes. 

But, in my opinion, she took the risk quite smartly. She had set an alarm that would go off around the ⅔ rd mark of the 3 hour walking tour. And that would be her trigger to end the walking tour wherever she was and book a cab to the airport.

If you’re wondering whether she missed her flight, then I would gently remind you that this series is titled What the Pho, Rosh and not WTP, M for a reason. 🤡

When her alarm rang, the entire walking tour crew were inside a big, fancy mall in the city centre. We were on a ten minute bio-break.

“Do you really have to go?” I whined to M as she turned her alarm off to book a cab and headed towards the entrance. 

She looked up with a yearning smile. “Yes, love. I also wish I could have stayed longer.”

PING! Her Grab ride was here.

“Alright, come. Let me drop you off to the cab at least” I offered and followed her to the entrance. Or what I thought was the entrance.

Once M left and I turned around, I was confused which way the washroom was. 

Right. I think it is a good time to confess to my readers that I am slightly directionally challenged. Google Maps on my phone and M in real-life are the reason I get to many unexplored places on time.

By the time I found the washroom the rest of the walking tour was nowhere to be found. 

Shit. Not again.

“Forget about the rest of the tour, don’t get lost. Book a cab to the Airbnb” M advised when I called her about the situation. 

Hmpf

Stubborn is not how I would normally describe myself. Persistent  is how I would correct someone if they described me so.

I wasn’t ready to give up yet. I stood in the middle of the lobby of that fancy mall and tried calling the number listed in the walking tour invitation. No answer.

I tried again. This time, the voices in my head answered the call instead.

entry.title: TIL: OpenType CFF Widths
entry.content:
Why a patched font can look fine on macOS and break on Windows.

Recently, I added a toggleable GTA display font to this site (check out the small lever at the bottom).

The only issue was that it didn’t have a µ glyph, so µblog fell back to monospace for just the first letter. I patched a matching µ directly into the font by cloning its u and extending the left stem down.

I was pleased by the font and everything looked great on macOS! I then checked it on Windows and noticed there was space between the glyph and the next character.

Apparently, OpenType CFF fonts store a glyph’s advance width1 in two places: the hmtx spacing table (which had the right 575) and optionally as an extra first number inside the glyph’s Type 2 CFF CharString2. The catch is that this number isn’t the actual width, it’s an offset added on top of a base width (Private.nominalWidthX).

In this font, defaultWidthX is 575 and nominalWidthX is 541. I originally put [575, 30, -199, 'rmoveto', ...], thinking 575 was the advance width. Since rmoveto only expects two numbers (x, y), that extra 575 was read as a width offset, making it 541 + 575 = 1116 instead of 575.

macOS’s CoreText uses hmtx and just ignores the bad width which was hiding our bug completely. Windows (DirectWrite) validates the Type 2 CFF CharString much more strictly and fails over it.

The fix was just dropping that first 575 ([30, -199, 'rmoveto', ...]). When a glyph’s width already matches defaultWidthX, you just leave that number out and let it inherit 575 directly.

Good reminder to check fonts on multiple OS and browser combinations!

#Footnotes

  1. It basically defines the horizontal spacing step for each glyph. ↩

  2. A tiny list of drawing instructions (move, line, curve) inside the font that traces a letter’s shape. ↩

entry.title: Week of November 15, 2026
entry.content:
It’s been a while, hasn’t it? Let me casually skip over the last six months and jump into the past week.

The week started off with no major fuss1. A badminton session that I’d planned had to be cancelled, so I went on a sidequest with @Messi instead. That did mean visiting previously unexplored areas of the city in public transportation, so I cannot complain. In this house, we appreciate public transportation.

Meta

Past me owes Present me an explanation because what are these Cloudflare cache rules, bro? After days of deliberation, I spent some time to recreate my caching rules, and everything is working as expected. Better, even.

Pushed out two new “features” this week.
1. For some reason, the canonical URL for most pages was either missing or set incorrectly. I’ve fixed that now, so hopefully Google Search Console stops complaining.
2. I’ve created a People page, inspired by the Character page that Thejesh has. Now that it’s live, all I need to do is backfill the info, which I will get to. One of these days2.

Life

Not a good start to the week - lack of sleep left me feeling a bit cranky on a couple of days. Those days felt like they whizzed by without me being productive. I often have to force myself to accept that not every day will be productive, and it’s okay. Wasting a couple of minutes here and there on social media3 is the main contributor to these feelings of not being productive. I’ve been doomscrolling quite a lot recently, so now feels like a good time to do a social media detox.

I’m usually one to shy away from the process of organizing birthday meet ups for friends, because I personally find the logistics of it all is a hard nut to crack. It’s something I’ve not done in so long. That being said, @Swetha4 and I spent a lot of time prepping things for @Messi’s birthday. After a lot of back and forth and some (unnecessary) anxiety on my part, nearly everything went as expected, including the little surprise we’d planned for her. An enjoyable couple (throuple?) of hours was had in the company of people I love spending time with, so it was all worthwhile. The price of community is inconvenience, and all that.

Work

Bit of a meh week at work. Of late, work has started to feel like I am merely a shepherd who’s managing a couple of agents as they go frolicking about and making changes to the code. I would prefer if this were not the case, but expectations of velocity hamper me ironically. What certainly doesn’t help is that most other code is ‘written’ by coding agents, so unless I have my agent summarize the (often verbose) code, there’s no way I’m getting through any of it in a reasonable amount of time. I keep getting assigned the most mundane yet challenging (derogatory) tasks imaginable, so maybe that’s something I should discuss with my lead in the coming days. Friday saw an unusually high number of people in the office, and that made for a good segue into the weekend. All things considered, I did manage to close out this week with a clean state, so that’s a win in my book.

Health

  • Trial and error suggests my medication is causing the insomnia I’ve been experiencing since… I started taking the medication. The medication, combined with a coffee I had on Sunday evening5, meant that I was awake till 5:30 AM on Monday. I could only get some shut-eye from 6:30 to 8, so I skipped the office and worked from home.
  • I’ve noticed a lot of inconsistency in my workout regimen before, but I’ve been consistently doing weight training, getting cardio done, and hitting my daily step targets the past two weeks, especially this week. That consistency shows in my progression as well - I’m almost proud of myself.
  • I have begun trialing volume eating since there’s no other way my gluttonous ass can survive a caloric deficit diet based on portion reduction. It seems to be working well so far, based on a sample size of two (2) days (Thursday and Friday).
  • My dalliance with the ENT department continues. Met a new doctor this time, and there will no permanent relief without drastic measures in the foreseeable future. I exaggerate, but you get my point. I did however, get to experience a CT scan, so that’s definitely an addition to my novelty list.
  • Currently testing openGym as a potential alternative to Hevy, on PikaPods. Kinda crazy how I’m ready to pay PikaPods to run a Hevy alternative because I don’t want to get the Hevy subscription!

Media

Not a lot of media consumption this week. I was too distracted the whole week to listen to podcasts, too lazy to watch a movie, and too tired to read. Progress on my current read has been slower than I would have liked. The days have been whizzing by, and if I were being honest, I kinda miss reading physical books. 8 of the last 10 books I read were paperbacks, not ebooks, and now I find reading on my Kobo a sluggish experience. I’m not entirely moving back to reading physical books, since acquisition, storage, and maintenance are all headaches I would like to avoid. But yeah, the spark is missing for now.

I did manage to get through a couple of items in my read-it-later list.

  • Can I just say that everything sucks?: This post by Divjot resonated hard because it captures all of the major pain points I’ve been trying to articulate for some time now. It’s frustrating living through These TimesTM, but Divjot didn’t succumb to the apathy that I unfortunately went through briefly.
  • Even Death is a Calling: A collection of notes from HImanshi’s reading of Albert Camus’ The Myth of Sisyphus. I have a cursory understanding of the absurd as Camus describes it, so these notes serve as a good starting off point for me if when I pick up The Myth of Sisyphus.

Food

Tried a couple of new places over the week, but nothing worth writing about here. Visited Casa Fresco nearly two years after my first visit, and it seems like they’ve relocated. The new place is… so-so, and I’ll leave it at that.

That’s it for this week. Hoping I keep this going consistently, or at least manage to write something for once.

  3. Instagram, ffs. ↩

  4. Is it obvious I’m excited about the People feature? ↩

  5. A mistake in retrospect. ↩

entry.title: Shifting From Linux to macOS
entry.content:
This post was first a rant. A long one, going on about how limited macOS is and how “stupid” every single design choice is. It was a Linux tinkerer crashing out because he was used to the freedom of doing and customizing anything and everything on his system, to the point of sometimes corrupting his OS and having to re-install it from scratch. ¶

I’m still that tinkering kid and I’m still quite annoyed, but I think I’ve found enough things to like about the MacBook (plus enough third-party apps that make the experience comfortable) that I’m fine, for now. So this is me documenting what made macOS comfortable for me, and create a new but familiar home. ¶

This post is dedicated to Accessibility Services, which — apart from heroically opening up software use to people with disabilities — make even the most locked down systems somewhat customizable for the general public. ¶

Also, from time to time, I’ll attach parts of my original rant like so.

What I Love Like

1. Hardware Shenanigans

You could say the hardware isn’t related to the operating system, but macOS is something that you can only experience properly on a MacBook. And the sleekness of the machine, the sharpness/color accuracy of the display, and precise/tactile nature of the components definitely makes it all come together. ¶

They really don’t mess around when they’re talking about Retina or ProMotion or whatever the latest one is called, because the colours of the display feel right. And the speakers — though they’re not something I’ll use often on a work laptop — create a sound stage that I’ve not experienced from laptops. Fitting all this into something this thin is a marvel of engineering. ¶

2. Touchpad & Gestures

This part, just by itself, has ruined my software experience on anything that’s not a MacBook. ¶

The touchpad is so intuitive, and so easy to click. I love how I can configure the “heaviness” of the click to be as much or as little as I want. I’m someone that usually opens the right-click menu (or closes tabs) by tapping with two/three fingers, but I enjoy the haptic feedback so much that I now click anyway. ¶

The gestures are so simple too, by the way. I was never one to use workspaces or “Virtual Desktops” on my machine before, but you could say the operating system has forced me to think in workspaces — and move maximized windows into a different space, to emphasize that they are a “big screen activity”. ¶

I love the surety of the multi-finger swipes. The physics of the windows/spaces moving around in response to my fingers is so well-made. I only learned recently (while trying to replicate this on KDE) that this does exist on my Linux machine, but the animations are much, much jankier. I watch KDE complete the action and I hear, “Waait, are you really sure you want this space to move away?” ¶

The scrolling experience also feels much smoother than it used to on Windows, back when I used it three years ago. I really like reading/viewing other people’s websites on the MacBook now. God, I have been spoiled. ¶

3. Battery & Performance

There’s this satisfaction I get when I open my laptop after a long time, and notice that the battery has not gone down as much as I’d anticipated. ¶

I already experienced this once when I shifted from Windows to Linux; because Linux does extremely well in saving energy. I really don’t know what Windows is doing though, maybe trying to spin the fans so fast that the laptop flies to Microsoft Headquarters and they can harvest your data. ¶

Anyway, the MacBook’s battery life does not disappoint. I’ve not experienced a single lag spike on the machine yet (touchwood) and don’t have to think about charging the laptop throughout my working day. I just keep the laptop plugged in when I’m at my desk and forget about it otherwise. ¶

4. One-Click Dictionary

I was just messing around with the touchpad haptics, when I learned that I can “deep click” a word anywhere to look it up in the dictionary. I then learned that I can select a longer phrase and do the same thing to look up the whole phrase. It’s instant too! ¶

This is great because I oftentimes skip trying to understand a word while reading, just because looking it up and coming back would lose me a lot of context. But having it a click away makes me more likely to stop and learn. This does make the experience of reading blogposts better too. ¶

5. Webcam Configuration

The webcam on the MacBook, from what I understand, is an ultrawide feed which they crop into. This means that the webcam is recording more of an area than it is showing you, and you can move the view around (in the Menu Bar settings) to position yourself in the feed as you like. ¶

This has helped me because I no longer have to center myself in the camera and instead just move the feed itself. There’s also Center Stage (which follows you around as you move), but I’d rather not turn it on because it can be distracting for other people during a meeting. ¶

Overall I’m just really happy with all the things I can tweak about the webcam feed system-wide, even if all I’ll really use it for is meetings. ¶

You might have noticed that most of these details relate more to the hardware, and less the software. Yeah…

What I Dislike

1. App Management

Alright so, the top left of each window has three buttons, right? Forget that they are on the left instead of the right like every other operating system. Now, when I click on the red icon with an “X” on it, what would you expect to happen? The app would close, yes? THEN WHY DOES THE APPLICATION STILL STAY OPEN?

When I brought this up with a long-time Mac user, they told me that this “app suspension” is what makes the macOS feel faster. But to me this entire system feels like an organizational nightmare. Every app that you “close” this way still remains on the dock with a dot underneath it, making me feel like it’s still open. ¶

And now that they can’t use that dot to denote a minimized window, they show minimized apps as an actual snapshot next to the Trash Bin. The app’s icon becomes even smaller next to the snapshot, making it hard to tell which app the window is from. Instead of remembering the icon of the app, I now have to remember what my minimized window looked like. Ugh. ¶

Thankfully, Cmd+Q and Cmd+W have become my closest friends here. They carry over pretty well to Linux as well, except I have to use Ctrl instead of Cmd. Oh, that reminds me— ¶

2. Mac’s Modifier Keys

On a typical laptop, the layout for the four buttons next to the Spacebar is Ctrl, Fn (Function), Meta/Super (Windows) and Alt. But on the Mac, it’s fn (Function), control, option and command. ¶

What in the mother of tarnation convinced these people that their buttons need to be different? The hell is the difference between Option, Command and Control? Also, there isn’t a Delete key and they just call the Backspace key “Delete”? How do I delete text on the right side of my cursor? Some messing around shows me that it’s now Fn+“Delete”, that’s good.

I’d seen tutorials and help articles that mentioned the Command key separately for Mac users when talking about shortcuts. But the placement of this key is so munted. Every piece of muscle memory that has pressed Ctrl for all these actions now has to press “Alt” in my head.

I thought I would just fix this by making the Control key act as the Command key, but guess what? Some apps have taken it upon themselves as their sole responsibility to use Control for their shortcuts instead of Command. Which means I have to keep both keys around. There is no escape.

Oh nevermind, there’s still an Escape key. Thank God.

The obliteration of my muscle memory is still a valid problem, but what I’m finding more difficult to grasp is the “buckets” Apple has used to distinguish between the functions of the keys. ¶

Usually, the Super key is used for shortcuts that are system-wide, Ctrl is for things inside the application that you’re looking at, and Alt is for everything else inside the application to reach via shortcuts. There are definitely exceptions where Alt+Tab and Super+Tab do the same thing, but it’s pretty straightforward overall. ¶

In contrast, it’s been a month since I got this machine and I cannot figure out the “buckets”. It doesn’t help that third-party applications are as confused as I am, and use Cmd for some actions and Control for others. In general I have to depend a lot more on finding things visually, which is not a great experience. ¶

3. Window Positioning/Sizing

I said before that I’ve gotten comfortable with how windows maximize into full screen, but I still have a bit of a rant left in me. I don’t know what Apple’s problem was, that led to the default behaviour of opening applications not be maximised windows. And even if they do, I don’t see why there’s a setting for them to just open maximised. ¶

This is one of the first things I spot when looking at a Mac user’s desktop — having an app open and still seeing information from so many different apps open behind it. The old me would have cried, but the Mac me knows I’m now complicit in their moral crime. ¶

Maximizing has become “Fill” and the maximize button makes windows full-screen. I have accepted that fate. ¶

4. Other Things

I don’t want to make a lengthy rant about every single problem so I’m just going to quickfire through them. ¶

  • The Finder (File Explorer?) is more like a canvas, instead of a grid? Like, dragging an item to a new empty space leaves its previous position empty. And you can just move things around like that. It sounds like another organizational nightmare.
  • The Spotlight Search, even though I’ve seen people rave about it, is actually quite slow in showing a list of options. I used to use KRunner on KDE, and that felt much faster than Spotlight.
  • The renaming shortcut for files on a Mac is literally pressing Enter, which weirds me out because “Enter” is usually short for “execute” in my head.
  • I can’t toggle Natural Scrolling separately for my touchpad and for my mouse. The setting applies to all connected devices, and now my mouse/touchpad scroll in opposite directions.

It’s all just a pile of inconveniences, and I don’t want to treat it as any more than that. But thankfully, there are tiny little applets out there that can solve some of them for me. I’ll list them out in-case they help out other people too. ¶

How I (Almost) Fixed It

1. Scroll Reverser

It’s hilarious to me that this is even a third-party utility, but I needed to fix the scrolling on my mouse and touchpad before I could continue setting up everything else. So this is just an applet that stays in the Menu Bar and lets you configure each device’s settings separately. ¶

The link to its website can be found here. ¶

2. Macuake

I use Yakuake on Linux to have a persistent drop-down terminal that can appear on any screen. So if I have a quick command to run (or have SSH’ed into a server and want to leave the connection open) then I can always have it present. ¶

I was missing that on macOS though, which is how I found Macuake a couple Reddit threads later. It has everything I needed from Yakuake, plus some clear tabs to allow opening multiple terminals. All of it is one Option+Space away. ¶

3. MiddleClick

I might have forgotten to mention, but I really liked how I could use a three-finger tap/click on Linux touchpads to close a tab (or open a link in a new one). KDE has a built-in option to make touchpads do this, but macOS is… built different. ¶

So now I have MiddleClick always open in the background. It’s a small open-source utility which is good, and sips very little battery. They have very minimal settings too — either to configure how many fingers make a middle-click, or to ignore certain applications from the service. ¶

4. Homebrew

With these utilities coming in from third parties (and macOS continuously making sure I knew the apps are downloaded from the Internet; like yes Apple, all apps come from the Internet), I knew I couldn’t depend on the App Store much longer. I also realized belatedly that the App Store wasn’t showing me the install prompt anymore, because it considered Macuake as an “overlaying application”. ¶

So it wasn’t long before I shifted my app management to be via Homebrew. I’m most likely not the first person introducing you to it, because it’s a very well-accepted CLI installer on macOS. It is to macOS what “pacman” or “yay” are to Arch Linux, so it makes me feel comfy to use too. ¶

5. Rectangle

The Apple ecosystem seems to have a rich community of third-party window managers that are trying to fill the space and make up for the disappointment that macOS has brought. The list of these window managers is loong, but one that comes well-recommended to me from people is Rectangle. ¶

It comes with every single keyboard shortcut you could possibly need in its free version, along with a paid version that includes cursor movements and some other extras. ¶

It’s actually configuration windows like these that I keep missing in Apple’s first-party experience; ones that lay all the settings bare and say, “Here you go, do what you want.” It’s a testament to what they think about the users and trust them with, and I’m currently finding their lack of trust a little offensive. ¶

6. AltTab

…Even after I close an app, the top left area still says the app’s name? And it still shows up in the list of apps when I do Alt+Tab? Scouring through some forums lets me know that this is intended behaviour and my laptop isn’t hanging; I’m just supposed to press Cmd+Q from now on.

Oh by the way, I seem to have said Alt+Tab before. I’m sorry, but there’s no Alt here. Who’s Alt?

Another little tidbit of the experience messing with me is switching between windows with Cmd+Tab. The switcher works between applications, but doesn’t really work when you have multiple windows of the same app open. In that case, there’s nothing you can do except open up Mission Control and vomit out all your open windows as tiny thumbnails on the screen. ¶

A great (and familiar) alternative that has worked out for me is AltTab, but the way it shows app thumbnails is by using the “screen recording” permission and recording snapshots of individual windows. It’s a good thing that the app is open-source, so you can go through and see how the source code uses that information. But the fact that someone other than Apple had to figure out this layout is really annoying. ¶

7. Tinycast

I already knew Spotlight Search wasn’t fast enough for me, and I’d heard of Raycast but knew it was closed-source. So I shifted directly to Tinycast, which is an open-source alternative to Raycast while being completely instant and not leaving me missing any features from KRunner. ¶

It lets me look through apps/files, remembers my clipboard history, lets me calculate things right in the search bar, and opens from the same shortcut that you normally use for Spotlight. Absolute legend. I also only know of this application because I saw someone from IndieWebClub write about it in their weeknotes. If I find that person, I’m going to edit this sentence! ¶

8. Amphetamine

KDE had this really easy button in its “Power & Battery” section, that let you suspend the device from sleeping until you disabled it again. I’ve used that toggle more recently (thanks to these darn LLM’s) but also to allow myself the time to zone out while not worrying about my laptop going dark and the activity I was doing going away. ¶

Amphetamine has really come in clutch to have that same functionality on the Mac, while still having a bunch of different controls that I’m never going to get into (because they’d be too complicated for me). Overall 10/10 recommend, but make sure you lock your laptops properly before leaving them and going away. :P ¶

9. Hidden Bar

Now, imagine that you have installed all these services and are using them on the daily. Since most of them stay alive by leaving an icon on your Menu Bar, you’ll soon see the top-right corner of your screen looking like this. ¶

Someone foresaw that too, and ended up creating something that might be one of the top items on this list. ¶

Hidden Bar essentially creates two items in your tray; an arrow icon and a partition icon. Anything dragged to the left of the partition will be hidden when the arrow is toggled, while everything on the right will remain visible. It’s a clever little piece that I’m glad to have, because it makes the desktop experience much cleaner. ¶

With that, the list is complete (for now). I’ve been using the final setup from this journey for a couple weeks now, and it’s safe to say that I’m comfortable with this new environment. Maybe even prefer it over Linux. But I’ll never admit that in public! And I’ll never forgive them for taking Ctrl of my muscle memory! ¶

I love the community of tinkerers that has come together in an attempt to make macOS their own, and I adore the creativity that every single app has portrayed. But it’s still quite upsetting that Apple has created a rather hostile environment for this software, all in an attempt to dumb down the system for the average user. ¶

If you find better alternatives to any of these problems, let me know. Maybe the solution we’ll all come to is installing Asahi on MacBooks. :D ¶

The wallpaper used in these screenshots is an aerial view of mountains taken by Inés Álvarez Fdez, and is free to use under Unsplash. ¶

entry.title: I Write Club (IWC) - Chapter One
entry.content:
My pen scribbled on the paper. I don't remember what I was writing. I only knew if I didn't write 2000 words, I would die.

3 MONTHS BACK

One evening, during my usual walks, I came across a pamphlet fallen on my path, on a otherwise clean and spotless road. It was very unusual. I picked it up not knowing that that one decision would change my life. The pamphlet had a big eye-catching font, black text on white paper, but instead of looking dull the words and the composition hypnotized me. It had stuff written on like, "WRITE YOUR HEART OUT!", Join I Write Club. Mandatory 1000 words a day commitment. “A person who lives by his words, dies by his words.”

I laughed, it seemed ridiculous. 

But, to tell the truth I had been struggling with writing consistently. Being a Copy Writer, I wrote for advertisements. But, my affair with writing seemed superficial. I wrote but only a few words everyday. But writing novels, telling stories, building characters and worlds that’s what I always aspired to do. That’s a completely different skill to Copy Writing. So I thought this might be interesting to checkout. The pamphlet had an address and the timing for next the club members meet. It was on weekends. 

The IWC was hosted on the remote part of the town. I assumed this was to save cost on renting the space. It was far out and I had struggled to find the place. It was buried in a manufacturing looking area of the town. The air was dusty and full of chemical smells. The few people I found looked lost too, apart from some laborers out an about, but overall the place looked barren.

When I found the address, it was a shopping complex, most of the shops shutters were down. A couple odd shops were open, some seemed like clinics of some sort, a repair shop, and an eatery. The address on the pamphlet said 3rd floor. The lift was out of service, so I took the stairs. The third floor only had a single open door at the end of the hallway.

When I entered the room, it was spacious and long. It had benches and tables that of the class room style. One could mistake this for a school classroom if not for the two personal office at the back and another room that looked like a pantry. But, I was most surprised by the people present in the room. There was no discernible pattern. It was the most random set of people I had seen in a group, almost like people where plucked out at random from a street. From teenagers to elders there were twenty some people present. Some talked in groups of two to four, others sitting alone or chatting with their bench mates. 

A girl who was talking with someone, seeing me walk in, came over to talk. She greeted me and introduced herself. 

"Hi, I'm Jacqualeen. Are you here for the I Write Club?" 

"Yes, I came across your pamphlet. I'm Ash, I would like to join the club."  

"Wonderful! We are staring in a few minutes. There's some new people joining today, so we'll briefly explain how IWC works, before our usual session starts. Please sit, and I’m so glad to have you here!" 

She smiled then walked towards the front to announce what she had just told me. So, I took up a seat on an empty bench further back. A few minutes later Jacqualeen introduced herself and started explaining how the club worked.  

She explained that new members have to write 2000 words per week and after 2 months if they don't skip a single week they can become full members, but full members have to write 1000 words everyday. But, if a new member fails to write 2000 words any week in the coming 2 months then they will be banned from the club. 

Someone interrupted her to ask, “What if a full member fails to write 1000 words a day? Suppose if they get writers block or something urgent comes up. Then what happens to their membership?” 

She smiled and said, “The rules are different for full members and they are only revealed to full members individually. After hearing the rules each member has the option to become a full member or leave the club. But that's all for later. Apart from writing sessions we have discussions on special topis every week. But first, the writing session. If you check there's a pen and paper in every desk drawer. Please take that and start writing. You'll be given 45 minutes to write. Minimum length should be 500 words.”   

A projector turned on and it presented 3 writing prompts on the wall. She said either we can write anything we wanted or use the prompts to get started. 

  1. Make a prayer to the goddess of knowledge

  2. Write the stream of consciousness of a writer

  3. A musician struggles to come up with lyrics for his next big song.

I found the prompts a bit odd. And, I was shocked that I had to write something on the spot with a time limit. Fortunately, I had an idea for a story floating around for sometime. This seemed like a good opportunity to put it to paper. 

The ABC Advertising agency had been struggling to retain clients after poor performance in the last 2 years. They had relied on their star lead/copywriter to come with creative campaign ideas. But, all his ideas preformed below average. Now their clients were threating to switch to their competitors. Losing a client is bad enough but they being snatched by a rival competitor is like a shark smelling blood is open waters. Their blood. Losing a single client could snowball into their downfall. But, a golden opportunity presents itself, there's a big client looking for an ad agency, onboarding this client can save them. This is also the last chance for the lead/copy writer to prove himself. 

David hasn't slept well in months. His eyes holds the tiredness and wariness of a convict out on the run. He comes to his office late and leaves at midnight. His office is a mess of papers, folders, and boxes of research and references lay unorganized. The agency's best lead/copywriter is sitting in his office holding is head in his hands when the phone rings. It's his boss. He says you've to meet with the client this afternoon for lunch to get the new campaign details. This client is a competitor of a famous cold drink conglomerate. He goes to meet the client. 

The meeting takes place at a business restaurant where most of the Ad executives always do big luncheons and meetings. They were seated on the corner booth near the window overlooking the city's skyline. He greets everyone. He is already acquainted with Micheal as he's the business executive, the rest he has meet in passing. This is a casual briefing before ppts, proposals, and money is involved. Micheal does a brief round of introductions. There's Tom, he takes care of finance, Baldwin who is the product director, and jerry who takes care of public relations. Baldwin said they want MadDrink advertised directly against Coco's energy drinks segment and this ad campaign they want to run nation wide. They will share all the product details, however, they want a solid proposal. They've already shared the same info with two competitors of ABC's and will be getting their proposals soon. Hearing this , David nodded and asked for more details and sales expectations and other things from the client. He asked pointed questions to each of them related to their department like budget allocations, product strengths and weakness, etc. When the meeting ended he shook hands with everyone and came back to office. 

He went over the product details. MadDrink is a carbonated drink with caffeine. It’s similar to hundreds of other carbonated caffeine drinks sitting on the shelf of all the supermarkets. He thought how will he run a nation wide campaign for a product that is identical to all it's competitors! It's like selling water! 

He called a team meeting, seating in the meeting room were the most talented, creative directors, copywriters and designers of the agency. He went over the client meeting and product details with everyone. Then the brain storming session started. 

Ring! Ring! Ring! 

I looked up and saw that the ringing sound coming from the speakers. Jacqualeen’s voice came from behind me, “Everyone the 45 minutes are up. I hope all of you were able to write 500 words. And, those who were unable to write have until 12am today to submit your work to our website, otherwise, you'll be banned from the club. Now, that the writing session is done. We will have a discussion about today's topic, Why Write!“

Thanks for reading and it you would like to share comments, feedback, or advice please feel free to use this google form.
